chapters.title: Advertisement.
paragraphs: This short treatise comes from a far larger work that I once began without properly judging whether my abilities were equal to it. I abandoned that project long ago. I have thought it appropriate to publish only this extract, as the part of the whole that seemed least open to objection.

chapters.title: Book I. Introduction.
paragraphs: In this treatise I intend to examine whether the nature of society allows government to operate by any settled and fair principles, taking human beings as they actually are and laws as they could be framed. Throughout the inquiry I shall try to keep natural right together with the public interest, so that what is just and what is useful never become separate concerns.

Having stated my aim, I shall begin without a speech about the subject's importance. Someone might ask what business I have writing about politics: am I a prince, or do I make laws? I hold neither position; that is precisely why I am writing. Were I a ruler or lawgiver, explaining what ought to happen would be a waste of my hours. I would put the necessary measures into effect myself, or else keep silent.

I was born a citizen in a free state and a participant in its supreme authority. However little my individual vote may affect public business, my entitlement to cast it is enough to make studying that business my duty. And I count myself fortunate that, as I examine the different kinds of government, each day supplies fresh grounds for admiring the government of my own country!
Geneva.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. I. The subject of the first book.
paragraphs: A human being enters life with freedom, yet subjection is found everywhere. A man may even imagine that he rules and owns other people when his own loss of liberty is only more conspicuous than theirs. How has this transformation come about? Can anything give it a legitimate basis? I cannot settle the first of these questions, but I believe I can answer the second.

If I considered nothing beyond power's existence and its effects, I would say this: while a people is forced into obedience, obeying is sensible; once resistance becomes possible, throwing off the restraint is better still. When they reclaim their freedom on the very ground on which it was taken away, either they are entitled to reclaim it, or those who took it never had an entitlement to do so. Yet society's very nature establishes an inviolable right on which every other right rests. Human beings do not receive it directly from nature, however: it rests on an agreement between them. Our inquiry must therefore turn to the kind of agreement this could have been. Before arguing that question, though, I need to establish the claims I have already put forward.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. II. On the primitive state of society.
paragraphs: The family is the oldest human association, and the sole association that arises from nature. Even within it, however, children remain bound to their father only for as long as his help is necessary to them. Once that need ends, the natural bond dissolves of itself. The children are released from their duty to obey him, just as he is released from his duty to care for them; each becomes independent of the other. They can certainly go on living together afterwards, but then their connection rests on choice rather than nature. Even the continuing union of a family therefore depends upon an agreement freely made by its members.

The freedom shared by all human beings necessarily follows from what we are. Self-preservation is the first law of our nature, and our foremost concerns consequently relate to ourselves. As soon as a person is old enough to exercise judgment, he alone is qualified to decide how his own preservation should be secured. He therefore becomes his own master.

We can thus find the earliest pattern of political association in the family. The father corresponds to its ruler, and his children to the people. All are born equally free, so any surrender of their freedom can be justified only by their shared interest. The difference between a family and a state amounts to this: a father's natural affection for his children rewards him for the care he gives them, whereas a ruler takes pleasure in exercising command. That pleasure replaces an affection for the people that the ruler does not possess.

Grotius disputes the view that governing power exists entirely for the advantage of the governed; he points to slavery as his example. Indeed, his usual procedure is to take what happens in practice as the foundation for what is right. A different method might have proved more convincing, though it could hardly have served tyrannical government better.

"Scholarly inquiries into natural and international law often amount merely to chronicles of longstanding abuses. To become excessively attached to studying them is therefore a ridiculous delusion." Manuscript Treatise on the Interests of France, by the Marquis d' A. That observation describes Grotius's case exactly.

On Grotius's account, then, it remains uncertain whether nearly all humanity belongs to roughly a hundred people, or whether that handful belongs to humanity as a whole. Throughout his work he seems inclined to the first position. Hobbes takes the same view. They accordingly divide our species into groups resembling cattle herds, with a keeper assigned to each. The keeper shields his herd from outsiders only so that he can claim it as his own possession.

A shepherd belongs to a higher order of being than the animals he tends. On the same reasoning, those who keep human herds—their rulers—must belong to a higher order than the people under their charge. According to Philo, this was Emperor Caligula's argument. His conclusion followed logically enough from the comparison: either rulers were divine beings, or the people they ruled were merely animals.

Caligula's reasoning closely resembles the arguments put forward by Hobbes and Grotius. Aristotle had already maintained, before either of those writers, that human beings were unequal by nature: some came into life destined for enslavement, while others were destined to exercise mastery.

Aristotle correctly described what existed, but treated its result as its cause. A man who enters life in enslavement is certainly born into a slave's condition. People living under it even cease to want freedom; they choose submission, just as Ulysses' companions chose their animal condition. If there are people who seem naturally enslaved, then, that is because they were first enslaved against nature. Force created the earliest slaves, and cowardice has kept slavery in existence.
Consult Plutarch's short treatise concerning the reasoning powers of animals.

I have left King Adam and Emperor Noah out of my discussion. Noah fathered three monarchs who divided the earth between them, like Saturn's children, with whom some have identified them. I hope I deserve a little credit for my restraint here. After all, I descend directly from one of those princes, probably through the family's eldest line. Who can tell whether a properly traced genealogy might establish me as the rightful successor to a monarchy embracing the whole world? However that may be, no one can dispute Adam's claim to rule the earth while he alone inhabited it: his claim was as sound as Robinson Crusoe's claim to his island in the equivalent circumstances. Their governments also enjoyed a considerable advantage. Each monarch could occupy his throne securely, with no danger of warfare, plots against him, or revolt.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. III. On the right of the Strongest.
paragraphs: Even the strongest cannot keep his mastery for ever through strength alone. He must turn his power into an entitlement to command, and turn submission into an obligation. From this comes the supposed right attached to superior strength: apparently a phrase used in mockery, yet in practice treated as an established principle. Will anyone ever give it its proper meaning? At its simplest, force is physical power, and I cannot see how its effects produce any moral claim. Giving way to greater force is something necessity imposes, rather than a voluntary act; at most it is a sensible precaution. How, then, can we describe it as a duty?

Still, let us briefly assume this alleged right exists, and see what insoluble absurdities follow. If possession of power establishes a right, any change in the cause changes the result. Each new power that exceeds the previous one inherits its supposed entitlement. People can therefore legitimately refuse obedience as soon as they can escape punishment for doing so. Since the right invariably belongs to the stronger party, their only task is to obtain the greater strength. But what sort of right disappears the moment its holder cannot enforce it? When obedience is secured solely through compulsion, declaring it a duty serves no purpose: when the compulsion ends, so does the obligation. In this argument, therefore, adding the word right to the word force contributes nothing. Right becomes a term with no meaning of its own.

We are told to obey the powers above us. If this instruction means submitting to greater force, it offers sound but unnecessary advice; I guarantee that such a rule will never be broken. I acknowledge that every power comes from God. Every bodily illness comes from that source too; does that forbid us to summon a doctor? Suppose a robber halts me on the road. Force obliges me to hand him my purse, but does conscience oblige me as well, even if I could keep it hidden from him? Hardly anyone would claim that. Yet the pistol pressed against my chest certainly represents a force greater than my own.

We must therefore reach this conclusion: power by itself establishes no entitlement, and our obligation to obey extends only to legitimate authority. Once again, the argument brings us back to the question with which I began.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. IV. On slavery.
paragraphs: Nobody possesses authority over other human beings by nature, and sheer power creates no entitlement to rule. Agreement between people must therefore provide the foundation for every legitimate exercise of authority.

Grotius asks: if one person can give up his freedom and place himself in slavery to a master, why should a people not collectively surrender theirs to a king? Several words in this proposition are ambiguous and need explaining, but I shall concentrate on alienation, or giving something up. What we alienate is transferred either as a gift or through a sale. A man who becomes another man's slave does not make a gift of himself: he sells himself, at least in exchange for his keep. But what would induce an entire people to sell themselves? A king does not provide his subjects with their livelihood; they provide his. And, as our friend Rabelais observes, a king needs a good deal to live on. Are subjects supposed to surrender their freedom on the understanding that whoever receives it may take their property too? I truly cannot see what would remain to them after that.

One may reply that a monarch preserves peace among his subjects. Granted; but what do they gain if his ambitious wars, his limitless greed, or his ministers' oppression destroy more than internal conflicts would? What have they gained if that very peace helps make them miserable? A prisoner may find his dungeon perfectly peaceful, but is that enough to make him satisfied with living there? The Greeks imprisoned in the Cyclops' cave were left undisturbed while each awaited his turn to be eaten.

The claim that a person can give himself away is both meaningless and absurd. Such a transaction would necessarily lack legal force and validity, if only because it would show that the person making it had lost his reason. To make the same claim about a people is therefore to imagine an entire nation losing its senses at once. Even if that happened, madness could establish no right.

Even supposing a man could give himself away, he could not dispose of his children on the same terms. As human beings they enter life free; that freedom belongs to them, and only they can decide what to do with it. Until they can exercise their own judgment, a father may indeed agree on arrangements for their preservation, acting in their name and for their security. But he cannot surrender them unconditionally and beyond recall. Such a gift would contradict nature's intention and overstep paternal authority. For arbitrary government to become legitimate, each succeeding generation would therefore have to remain free to accept or refuse its authority. Under that condition, however, it would cease to be arbitrary government.

Giving up the liberty we possess by nature means giving up our very existence as human beings: we abandon humanity's obligations along with its entitlements. What compensation could possibly repay someone who surrendered everything he had? Such a surrender contradicts our nature, since removing freedom from the will removes the moral character of our actions. An agreement granting unrestricted authority to one party and requiring unquestioning obedience from the other is therefore self-defeating and contradictory. How could we owe any reciprocal duty to someone from whom we were entitled to demand everything? Since nothing on his side could balance that claim, does this not necessarily make the agreement invalid? What could my slave claim from me when I owned both him and everything he possessed? Anything he claimed would already belong to me. The suggestion that he could assert such a claim against me is absurd.

Grotius, along with other authors, finds another origin for this alleged entitlement in success on the battlefield. Their reasoning is that the victor may execute the defeated man, who may in turn legitimately buy survival by giving up freedom. They regard this bargain as particularly justifiable because each side gains something from it.

Yet the alleged entitlement of a conqueror to dispose of defeated people's lives certainly does not follow naturally from warfare in any form. One reason alone makes that clear. While human beings lived in their original independence, their relations with each other lacked the permanence needed to establish either peace or war as a condition. People consequently cannot be enemies by nature. War originates in relations concerning things, rather than relations between persons. Because its basis is property rather than personal relations, war cannot exist between one man and another, either in natural life, where settled property does not exist, or in civil society, where laws secure everything.

Individual quarrels, clashes and duels do not establish a condition of war of this kind. As for the private combats permitted under the institutions of Lewis XI, King of France, these were simply abuses belonging to feudal government. That system was thoroughly absurd, conflicting as much with sound policy as with the principles of natural justice.

War therefore concerns states in their relations with other states. Individuals become enemies only incidentally, in their capacity as soldiers. Neither their humanity nor even their citizenship makes them enemies; their role is that of defenders of their community, rather than simply its members. A state's enemy, in other words, can only be another state, not individual men. Things that differ in their essential nature cannot stand in a common relationship of this kind.

The principle agrees, indeed, with accepted rules throughout history and with the unvarying conduct of every civilized nation. Announcements that war has begun are intended chiefly for subjects' information, rather than for the information of their sovereigns.

An outsider may be a ruler, an ordinary person or a whole nation: if he plunders a subject, kills him or makes him a prisoner without announcing war upon his prince, his conduct is robbery rather than enemy action. Even when hostilities are underway, a prince acting justly may take the public possessions of the hostile country but will leave private people and their belongings secure. He thereby acknowledges the entitlements that support his own position. Warfare seeks the destruction of a hostile state. It permits the killing of that state's armed defenders; once those defenders give up their weapons, however, they no longer act as enemies or agents of hostility. Their status is simply that of human beings, and murdering them has no justification whatsoever. Indeed, destroying a state can sometimes be achieved without killing even a single person belonging to it. No wartime privilege can extend beyond what accomplishing war's purpose requires. Admittedly, Grotius does not supply these principles, nor do citations from poets establish their authority. They are conclusions reason draws from the matter's own nature.

The supposed entitlement arising from conquest has no basis except force—the rule that assigns everything to superior strength. But if victory in war gives no permission to slaughter the defeated, this nonexistent permission cannot establish a right to enslave them. If killing an enemy is permissible only when force cannot reduce him to slavery, permission to enslave him can never be based on permission to kill him. It is consequently an unjust bargain to charge him his freedom for a life we have no right to take. To ground a power of life and death in a right to enslave, and then ground the right to enslave in that power of life and death, plainly traps us in circular reasoning.

Suppose, nonetheless, that this appalling entitlement to wholesale slaughter did exist. I still maintain that a person enslaved through defeat in war, or a conquered nation reduced to slavery, owes the master nothing except obedience while he can enforce it. By accepting something in exchange for their lives, the victor does them no kindness. Instead of destroying them by useless killing, he merely adopts another form of destruction that benefits him. He therefore acquires no additional authority over them; the condition of war continues exactly as before. Their relationship is its evident consequence, and his exercise of wartime rights shows that no peace treaty has replaced it. Someone may insist that they have reached an agreement. Very well: that agreement amounts to a truce. Far from terminating the war between them, it necessarily assumes that the war continues.

However we approach the question, then, the supposed entitlement to enslave people has no validity: it is not merely unjust but absurd and meaningless. Slavery and justice contradict one another; either excludes the other. The following offer would accordingly be equally ridiculous whether addressed by one private person to another or by an individual to an entire people: I propose an agreement whose costs fall entirely on you and whose benefits are entirely mine. I shall keep it for as long as it suits me, and you must keep it for as long as I choose.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. V. On the necessity of recurring always to the primitive convention.
paragraphs: Even if I conceded everything I have so far refuted, the defender of despotism would gain little. Bringing a multitude into subjection remains very different from governing an associated people. Suppose any number of individuals, taken separately and one after another, fall under one man's control. We have only slaves and their master, not a people with its leader. Call them an accumulation if you like; they still do not form an association. Neither a commonwealth nor a political body exists among them. Even if the master acquired half the globe, he would remain a private person. His interest, distinct and separate from theirs, would remain purely private too. At his death, moreover, the empire he controlled would dissolve, leaving its parts wholly disconnected, as an oak becomes a pile of ashes when fire consumes it.

Grotius says that a people can voluntarily give themselves to a king. His own statement therefore implies that they already constitute a people before surrendering to royal authority. Even this supposed gift is a social act: it assumes that they have publicly considered the question. Before examining the act through which a people choose their king, we should consequently investigate the act through which they became a people at all. This earlier act necessarily precedes the other, and supplies society's true foundation.

Without an agreement made beforehand, why should the smaller group be bound to accept what the larger group chooses—except, of course, where everybody has voted alike? Imagine a hundred people who want a master and ten who do not. What entitles the hundred to decide for those ten? Majority voting itself rests on an agreed arrangement. It therefore assumes that the participants have, on at least one occasion, all been of one mind.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. VI. On the social pact or covenant.
paragraphs: Imagine that humanity has reached a point where the obstacles to surviving in natural independence exceed what individuals can overcome through their own efforts. At that critical moment the original condition of human life could no longer continue. Unless human beings changed how they lived, their species would have perished.

Human beings cannot bring new powers into existence; they can only combine and direct powers that already exist. Their sole means of survival is therefore to unite, gathering sufficient force to overcome the obstacles threatening their security, and setting it in motion through an initiating power that can make its parts act together.

This combined power requires many separate forces to cooperate. Yet each person's strength and freedom are his main means of preserving himself. How can he commit them to the common interest without damaging his own interests and neglecting what he owes himself? Applied to our present inquiry, this difficulty becomes the problem stated immediately below.

"We must find a form of association that defends and protects the person and property of every member with the entire strength of the community, and under which each individual, though joined with all the others, still obeys no one but himself and remains as free as he was before." That is the basic problem, and the social compact is its solution.

The terms of this compact follow so strictly from the nature of the act that the smallest restriction or change would void them and leave them without effect. Even if they were never formally announced, they are identical everywhere and are everywhere tacitly acknowledged and accepted. Once the pact is broken, however, each person returns to his natural liberty and regains his original rights, since he forfeits the agreed liberty for whose sake he had surrendered them.

Taken together, the terms come down to one: each person transfers himself, with every right and privilege, to the community as a whole. Because everyone gives himself completely and holds nothing back, all stand on equal ground; no one benefits by making their common bond oppressive to another.

Because nothing is reserved, the union can be complete and no member keeps a special claim. If each retained private privileges, no common judge could settle disputes between an individual and the public. A person deciding some cases for himself would soon claim that role in every case. Natural independence would persist, and the association would become oppressive or fail.

Finally, whoever gives himself to the whole does not give himself to any particular person. He obtains over every other member exactly the entitlement he grants them over himself. He consequently receives an equivalent for what he contributes, together with greater power to safeguard what he keeps.

Remove everything inessential from the social compact, and its terms become these: "Together and individually, we who make this agreement place ourselves and our capacities under the supreme guidance of the will we share as a whole. Acting collectively, we accept every member as an inseparable part of that whole."

By this act of association, then, the many separate parties to the contract are turned into a single moral and collective body. That body has as many members as the assembly has votes, and the act itself gives it its unity and its existence. The public person produced by the joining of all its members used to be called a CITY, and now goes by the name of a republic or body politic. Its own members call it the state when it is passive, the sovereign when it is active, and a power when they set it beside other bodies of its kind. The associates as a group take the name of the people; one by one they are citizens, in so far as they share in the sovereign authority, and subjects, in so far as they are placed under the laws of the state. These words are often confused and used in place of one another, though it suffices to be able to tell them apart when precision is wanted.

Among modern people the true meaning of this word has almost wholly been lost: most take a town for a city, and a householder for a citizen. They do not understand that houses make up a town, but only citizens make up a city. This same mistake once cost the Carthaginians dearly. In all my reading I do not remember finding the title Cives given to the subjects of a prince, not even to the Macedonians in the past, nor in our own time to the English, though they are nearer to liberty than any other nation. Only the French casually call themselves citizens, because they have no true idea of what the word means, as their dictionaries show; if they had, they would be guilty of high treason in using it. For them the word expresses a virtue rather than a privilege. So when Bodin wrote of the citizens and the inhabitants of Geneva, he made a wretched blunder by mistaking one group for the other. Mr. d'Alembert has avoided this error in the Encyclopoedia, where he correctly distinguishes the four orders of people (five, if mere foreigners are counted) found in our city, only two of which make up the republic. No other French author that I know of has ever grasped the meaning of the word citizen.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. VII. Of the sovereign.
paragraphs: The stated formula shows that association commits private persons and the public to obligations towards one another. Each participant enters an agreement with himself, if I may put it that way, and becomes bound in two capacities. His share in sovereign authority binds him towards particular individuals; his membership of the state binds him towards its sovereign. Here, however, we cannot apply the civil-law maxim releasing people from obligations they undertake to themselves. Promising something to oneself personally is very different from promising it to a collective whole in which one has a share.

Note a further point. Because every person is committed in two capacities, a public decision obliges the subjects toward the sovereign; for the very opposite reason, it cannot oblige the supreme power toward itself. It would therefore be inconsistent with what a political body is for its sovereign to enact a statute that it has no power to violate. Since the sovereign stands in a single relation only, it resembles an individual who tries to enter a contract with himself. From this we see that no fundamental law capable of binding the whole people exists or could exist, and the social compact is no exception. That does not prevent the body from entering into undertakings with outsiders on matters which leave the compact untouched; in dealing with the outside, it counts as one simple individual.

Yet the body politic, or sovereign, owes its very existence to this inviolable agreement. It cannot lawfully make any commitment, even to another body of the same kind, that conflicts with the original act's terms—for example, giving away part of itself or surrendering wholly to a foreign sovereign. Breaking the act that constitutes its existence would destroy that existence, and nothing can emerge from nothing.

Once numerous individuals unite in this way, an attack on any member necessarily attacks the entire body; still more plainly, an attack on the body injures its members. Both obligation and self-interest therefore require the two parties to support one another. The same people, acting in these two capacities, ought to seek all the advantages their double relationship can provide.

The sovereign consists solely of the individuals who make up the state, so it cannot have an interest opposed to theirs. The supreme authority consequently needs to provide its subjects with no guarantee: the body cannot harm all the members of which it consists. Later we shall see that it can no more tend towards harming any individual member. Its very existence thus necessarily makes the sovereign what it ought to be.

The subjects' relationship to the sovereign is different. Despite their common interest, the sovereign has no assurance that they will honour their commitments unless some means can be found to secure their faithfulness to them.

For every individual, as a human being, can have a private will that differs from, or runs contrary to, the general will that he holds as a citizen. His own interest may speak to him in a voice quite opposed to the common interest. He regards his existence as something complete and naturally independent, and so he may see what he owes the common cause as a voluntary gift, whose absence would harm others less than its payment would burden him. And because he does not take the moral person of the state to be a real being, since it is no man, he may wish to enjoy a citizen's rights without discharging a subject's duties. If this injustice grew, it would ruin the body politic.

To keep the social compact from being an empty formula, then, it carries an unspoken engagement, the only one able to give the rest their force. Anyone who will not obey the general will must be constrained to do so by the entire body. All this means is that he is to be forced into freedom. This is the very condition that, by handing each citizen over to his country, frees him from all personal subjection. It is the device on which the whole political machine turns, and it alone makes civil engagements legitimate. Without it they would be absurd, despotic, and exposed to the grossest abuse.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. VIII. Of civil society in general.
paragraphs: Passing from natural independence into organized society profoundly changes a human being. Justice replaces instinct as the rule of conduct, and actions acquire a moral character they previously lacked. When the call of duty takes the place of bodily impulses and the rule of appetite, someone who formerly considered only his own gratification discovers that he must act on other principles. He must consult reason before following his passions. Joining society certainly deprives him of many advantages belonging to natural life. But the advantages he receives in exchange are immense: his faculties find employment and develop, his ideas widen, his feelings become nobler, and his whole spirit rises to a higher level. Unless abuses within this new condition drag him below his former one, he ought continually to bless the fortunate moment that rescued him from it. That moment transformed him from an unthinking, ignorant animal into a being capable of intelligence and wisdom.

Let us reduce the exchange to simple terms so that its profit and loss can be compared. In making the social compact, a man surrenders his natural liberty, his unrestricted right to anything that attracts him and lies within his reach. In return he is granted civil liberty, along with ownership of everything he holds. Lest we be mistaken about these two sides of the bargain, we must distinguish between natural liberty, limited by nothing except the individual's own strength, and civil liberty, restrained by the general will. A parallel distinction separates possession, which merely follows from strength or from being first on the spot, and property, which only a positive legal title can establish.

Moral liberty could be added to what the civil state brings, for it alone makes a man the true master of himself. To be moved by appetite alone is to be a slave; to obey a law we have set for ourselves is to be free. I have already dwelt on this longer than I should, because what philosophers mean by liberty is not our present topic.

chapters.title: Book I. CHAP. IX. Of real demesnes.
paragraphs: On joining the community, each member commits himself to the public as he then stands, with all his powers and capacities, including the possessions that form part of those capacities. This does not mean that transferring possession changes its nature, turning it into genuine property in the sovereign's hands. Rather, because the community's strength is incomparably greater than an individual's, public possession is in practice more secure and harder to reverse, without becoming more legitimate—at least in relation to foreigners. In relation to its own members, every state controls their possessions by virtue of the social compact, which provides the foundation for all other rights within it. In relation to other powers or states, however, its claim rests only on first occupation, a claim it receives from the individuals concerned.

A claim based on occupying something first has more substance than one based on superior force, but becomes a just entitlement only after property has been established. Nature gives every person a claim to whatever he needs to live. Yet the definite act that makes him the owner of a particular holding excludes him from ownership of other holdings. Once his share has been allotted, he should restrict himself to it, and can no longer claim common possession of everything. This explains why first occupation, which counts for little in natural life, commands such respect in society. In considering the claim, our attention is directed chiefly towards what belongs to someone else, rather than simply towards what is not ours.

In general, a claim based on first occupation requires the following conditions. First, the land in question must not already be occupied by anybody else. Second, the area occupied must be no larger than the occupants need to support themselves. Third, taking possession must involve actual cultivation, rather than an empty ceremony. Where legal titles are lacking, cultivation is the only indication of property deserving recognition.

To grant the first occupant a right to as much land as he can cultivate and needs for his support is surely to carry the matter as far as reason allows; otherwise there is no way to set limits to this right. Is it enough for a man to set foot on uninhabited ground to claim at once that it is exclusively his? Is it enough that he is strong enough, at one moment, to drive others off, to take from them forever the right to return? How can a man, or a whole people, take over an immense territory and shut out the rest of mankind without committing an unlawful usurpation, since they thereby deprive everyone else of a dwelling place and of the means of living that nature gave to all in common? When Nunez Balbao stood on the shore and in the name of the crown of Castile took possession of the Pacific Ocean and all of South America, was that enough to dispossess all the inhabitants of that vast country and shut out every other sovereign in the world? On that assumption such empty ceremonies could have been multiplied absurdly, and his Catholic Majesty would have had nothing more to do than take possession of the whole world from his study, and then strike from his empire only those lands already held by other princes.

It is easy to understand how neighbouring individual estates, joined together, become public territory. Sovereign authority extends from the subjects to their holdings and thus acquires a claim over both people and land. This places possessors in the greatest dependence, making even their own resources a guarantee of their loyalty. Ancient rulers seem not to have appreciated this advantage fully. Calling themselves kings of the Persians, Scythians or Macedonians, they apparently regarded themselves as leaders of people rather than masters of a country. Modern princes show greater cunning in calling themselves kings of England, France, Spain, and so forth. By claiming the territory itself, they make sure of its inhabitants.

One striking thing about this transfer is that the community, in taking over what individuals own, does not plunder them at all. It merely guarantees them their possessions, turning wrongful seizure into lawful right and mere holding into ownership. The owners come to be seen as keepers of the common wealth, their rights are honoured by all the members and defended by the whole force of the state against outsiders, and so, through a surrender that profits the public and themselves still more, they obtain, one might say, everything they handed over. The apparent contradiction dissolves once we separate the rights that sovereign and owner each hold over the same property, as will appear below.

It may also happen that people unite in society before owning anything at all, and then, taking over a stretch of land large enough for everyone, either enjoy it in common or divide it among themselves, in equal parts or in whatever proportion the sovereign decides. However the acquisition comes about, each individual's right over his own estate must always yield to the community's right over the estates of all. Without that, the social bond would have no strength, and the exercise of sovereignty no real power.

I shall close this book with an observation that should underpin the entire social system. Far from abolishing human beings' natural equality, the founding compact establishes moral and legal equality to compensate for their natural and physical differences. People may possess unequal bodily strength and unequal intellectual abilities, yet agreement and right make them equals within the association.

Under some governments this equality is only a deceptive appearance, serving to keep poor people miserable and to favour oppression by the rich. Laws in fact always benefit those with wealth and injure those who have nothing. Society therefore benefits humanity generally only when everyone owns something and no individual among them possesses an excessively large share.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. I. That the sovereignty is unalienable.
paragraphs: The first and most important conclusion from the principles established so far is this: only the general will can guide the state's forces towards the purpose for which it was founded, namely the common good. Conflicting private interests may have made society necessary, but agreement between those interests must have made society possible. Its bonds must have arisen from something those different interests shared; without any point at which they could be reconciled, no society could have existed. Those shared points alone, therefore, should provide the basis on which society is governed.

Sovereignty, I maintain, consists only in exercising the general will and therefore cannot be handed over. The sovereign is a collective being, which can speak for itself alone: a people can transfer or delegate its power, but cannot transfer its will.

It is not strictly impossible for a private will to agree with the general will of a whole people on some single point; but it is impossible for that agreement to be constant and lasting, since the private will tends toward favouritism and the general will toward complete equality. It is still more impossible to be sure that such agreement would continue, even supposing it could, because it would arise by accident rather than by design. The sovereign can declare that it currently wills what a particular man wills, or what he says he wills; it cannot declare that it will will whatever he wills tomorrow, for it is absurd that a will should shackle itself for the future, and no will can consent to anything against the good of the being that possesses it. If a people, therefore, merely promised obedience, that very act would strip it of its character as a people and dissolve it. The moment a master appears, there is no sovereign, and the body politic is destroyed.

This does not mean that a chief's commands cannot be treated as expressions of the general will where the sovereign leaves them unopposed despite remaining free to contradict them. In those circumstances, the people's universal silence can be taken as consent. I shall explain this point further towards the end.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. II. That the sovereignty is indivisible.
paragraphs: Collective judgment, taken as a whole, points toward shared advantage and is therefore right. That does not guarantee that a crowd reasons correctly in every discussion. People want what benefits them, but may misidentify it. The people cannot be corrupted as a body; it can be mistaken, and in those moments may seem to choose its own harm.
Generality does not always require unanimous agreement. It does require that every person be allowed to cast a vote: excluding anyone by formal rule damages the will's general character.

Unable to divide sovereignty at the level of its basic principles, our political writers divide it according to the matters it deals with. They distinguish will from power, legislation from execution, the powers of taxation from those of administering justice or conducting war, and domestic business from foreign affairs. Sometimes they jumble these together; sometimes they treat each as separate. Their sovereign becomes a fantastical composite, like a man put together from several bodies, one consisting entirely of eyes, another entirely of arms, a third entirely of feet. Japanese conjurers, we are told, cut up a child before their audience and toss the severed limbs into the air, one after another. The pieces reunite and the child comes down alive and unharmed. Our modern political writers perform much the same feat. Having skilfully dismembered the political body, they bring its pieces together again by magic and announce that it is just what it was before.

Writers fall into this error because they lack exact ideas about the sovereign authority and take its mere consequences for components of its essence. Consider how acts of declaring war and making peace are commonly counted as acts of sovereignty. They are not, since neither is a law; each is only the application of one, a particular act deciding what the law means in the case at hand. That will become plainer after we have fixed the sense of the word law.

Examining their other divisions in the same way reveals the same mistake whenever sovereignty appears to be divided. The powers supposedly forming its separate parts are all subordinate to it. They presuppose an earlier decision by a higher will, whose determination those powers serve merely to carry out.

One cannot say how much confusion this lack of exactness has brought to the arguments of political writers when they have tried to judge, from the principles they had laid down, the respective rights of kings and peoples. In chapters three and four of the first book of Grotius anyone can see how that learned man, and his translator Barbeyrac, entangled themselves in their own sophisms, fearful of claiming too much or too little for their cause, and of setting at variance interests they were bound to reconcile. Grotius was unhappy with his native land, had taken refuge in France, and wished to flatter Lewis XIII, to whom his work is dedicated; so he spared no art or trouble to strip the people of their rights and to clothe kings in privileges. Barbeyrac did likewise, dedicating his translation to George I of England. Unluckily, the expulsion of James II, which he calls abdication, forced him to be cautious, to evade and equivocate, so as not to make William III a usurper. Had these two authors held to the true principles, every difficulty would have vanished and they would have been consistent; but they would then have been obliged to tell the plain truth and to please only the people. And truth is no road to fortune: the people give out no ambassadorships, no offices, no pensions.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. III. Whether the general Will can be in the wrong.
paragraphs: It follows from the foregoing that the general will is always upright and always tends toward the public good; it does not follow that the people's deliberations are always equally upright. We always desire our own good, but we do not always discern it. A people is never corrupted, though it is often deceived, and only when it is deceived does it appear to will something harmful.

What every member wills, added together, often differs considerably from what the whole body wills generally. The general will looks solely to shared interests; the other total reflects individuals' private interests and simply adds their separate wishes together. Remove from that total the opposed wishes that cancel one another, however, and the differences left over, taken together, form the general will.

The Marquis d'A. remarks that different interests proceed from different principles: two separate interests may join forces because both oppose a third. He might equally have remarked that everyone's interests join forces by opposing each person's individual interest. If interests neither differed nor clashed, the common interest would face no obstacle and would scarcely be perceptible as such. Affairs would run smoothly by themselves, and the management of civil society would no longer be an art.

If a people that was adequately informed deliberated without any dealings among its citizens, the general will would always arise out of the great number of slight differences, and the resolution would always be good. But once intrigues arise and partial associations form at the cost of the large one, the will of each such association becomes general for its members and particular for the state. One could then say that the number of voters is no longer the number of men, but only the number of associations. Differences are then fewer, and the result is less representative of everyone. If a single faction becomes large enough to overbear all the rest, the result stops being the total of numerous minor differences and becomes the product of one major difference. At that point there is no general will left.

If the general will is to be expressed, then, it is essential that the state contain no partial societies and that each citizen form his opinion for himself alone. This was the sublime system of the great Lycurgus. If partial societies cannot be avoided, their number should be multiplied and their inequality prevented, as Solon, Numa, and Servius did. Only such measures can ensure that the general will stays informed and that the people are not misled about their own interest.

Machiavel says: It is true that some divisions damage republics while others help them. Those accompanied by factions and partisan followers do damage; those maintained without factions or partisan followers help. Since a republic's founder cannot ensure that no hostilities arise within it, he must at least ensure that factions do not arise. History of Florence, book vii.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. IV. Of the limits of the sovereign power.
paragraphs: Take the state, or city, to be nothing but a moral person, one that lives by the joining together of its members, and whose weightiest duty is to keep itself in existence. Such a being needs a force reaching everywhere and able to compel, so that it can set each part in motion and order it in the manner most favourable to the welfare of all. Nature gives a man complete power over his limbs; in the same way the social compact gives the body politic complete power over all of its members. Under the guidance of the general will, this power is what bears, as I have already remarked, the name of sovereignty.

Beyond this public person, though, we have to take account of the private individuals who compose it, and whose life and liberty are by nature independent of it. We now have to separate the rights of citizens from those of the sovereign, and the duties that citizens owe as subjects from the natural rights they hold as human beings.
Careful reader, do not hurry to charge me with a contradiction here. The poverty of language makes it impossible for me to avoid an apparent clash of terms. Be patient for a little while.

It is agreed that, under the social compact, a person gives up only those parts of his power, property, or liberty whose use matters to the community. Yet it must also be admitted that the sovereign alone is qualified to judge what matters in this way.

A citizen must render the state every service he can possibly give whenever the sovereign calls on him. The sovereign, for its part, may demand nothing from a subject that serves no public purpose; nor could it even wish to do so. Under the laws of reason, as under those of nature, nothing happens without a cause.

Our obligations to the social body are binding only because they run both ways; and by their nature we are unable, in meeting them, to work for others without working for our own benefit too. What explains the general will's constant rightness, and everyone's steady wish for the happiness of each? Only this: there is no one who does not take the word each to mean himself, and who does not consider his own interest while voting for the interest of all. Several things follow. Equality of right, and the idea of justice that goes with it, derive from the preference each person naturally has for himself, and so from human nature. To deserve its name, the general will has to be general in what it aims at just as in where it comes from. It must proceed from everyone if it is to apply to everyone. And it loses its natural correctness when it bears on some single, definite object, because then we are judging a matter outside ourselves, with no authentic standard of fairness to direct us.

As soon as a particular fact or right is at stake, one about which no earlier general convention exists, the affair turns into a dispute. It is a lawsuit in which the private persons concerned form one party and the public the other, and I can see in it no law to be followed and no judge to give a ruling. Referring it to a formal decision of the general will would be ridiculous, since that decision could only be the conclusion of one of the parties, and would therefore look to the other like something external and partial, tending toward injustice and exposed to error. Just as a private will cannot represent the general will, so the general will changes its nature when directed at a particular object, and cannot, as general, rule on a man or a fact. Think of Athens: its people undertook to choose or dismiss its rulers, to give distinctions to one man and punishments to another, and through a great mass of separate decrees performed every function of government indiscriminately. Acting like this, it had ceased to possess a general will in the proper meaning of the term; they acted as magistrate, not as sovereign. This goes against received opinion, but give me time to set forth my own.

We can see from this that the general will depends less on how many votes are cast than on the shared interest that brings them together. Under this arrangement, everyone necessarily accepts the same conditions that he sets for others. That is why interest and justice fit together so remarkably, and why public declarations carry a quality of fairness. It disappears when a particular case is debated, because then there is no common interest to make the judge’s standard match the party’s.

Whichever way we go back to the first principle, we arrive at the same result: the social compact creates among the citizens an equality so complete that all of them undertake duties on identical conditions and all should have the same benefits. Given the nature of the compact, each act of sovereignty, which is to say each genuine act of the general will, lays the same burden on every citizen or grants the same benefit to every one. Hence the sovereign is acquainted only with the nation as a body, and distinguishes none of the persons who compose it. What, then, strictly counts as an act of sovereignty? It is not an agreement between a superior and an inferior; it is an agreement made between the body as a whole and every single member of it. Such a pact is lawful, because the social contract underlies it; just, because all share in it; advantageous, because it can have no object but the general welfare; and secure, because public force and supreme authority stand behind it.

So long as subjects are bound only by agreements of this kind, they obey nobody but their own will; and to ask how far the sovereign's rights and the citizens' rights extend is to ask how far citizens may commit themselves to one another, each toward all and all toward each.

We can therefore see that sovereign power, though absolute, inviolable, and sacred, cannot go beyond the limits of these general agreements. Everyone remains free to dispose as he pleases of the liberty and property that those agreements leave at his disposal. The sovereign has no right to burden one subject more heavily than another, since such a measure would concern a particular case in which the sovereign has no authority to act.

Once these distinctions are accepted, it is plainly wrong to say that individuals truly give anything up when they enter the social compact. Their position improves because of it. They do not surrender what they have; they trade an uncertain and precarious way of life for one more stable and secure. They exchange natural independence for social liberty, the ability to harm others for protection against harm, and their own natural strength—which others might overcome—for a civil power made irresistible by union. The state continually protects even the lives citizens have pledged to it. When they must risk death in its defence, they merely return to society what they previously received. By risking their lives for their country, they do no more than they would have had to do more often, and at far greater danger, in the state of nature, where unavoidable attacks would force them to defend their means of survival with their lives at stake. Everyone is indeed obliged to fight for the country, but the laws spare each person the need to fight for his own protection. Surely people gain overall when they share some risks for common security that each would otherwise face alone Their shared protection rests on their equal place within the civic body.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. V. On capital punishments.
paragraphs: A puzzle is often raised: individuals cannot lawfully dispose of their own lives, so how could they pass such a right on to the sovereign? The question seems hard to answer only because it is badly posed. Each man has the right to run risks with his life in order to preserve it. Did anyone ever charge a man with suicide for throwing himself from a window to escape a fire? And has anyone blamed a man drowned in a shipwreck for having known about the dangers of the sea when he went aboard?

The social compact aims to preserve those who make it. Anyone who wants its benefits must accept the means that go with them, including some dangers and losses. A person who would save himself at the expense of others must put himself at risk for their safety when needed. The citizen no longer decides for himself what danger the law requires him to face. But if the ruler declares that the state’s welfare requires his life, he must yield it: his security has always depended on these terms, and his life comes conditionally from the state as well as from nature.

The death penalty for criminals can be understood in the same way. To prevent an assassin from taking our lives, we agree that our own may be taken if we become assassins. This agreement does not give our lives away; we enter it for our protection. We cannot suppose that anyone joined it with a settled plan to be hanged in such cases.

Besides, any malefactor who strikes at his country's law turns, by his offences, into a rebel and betrayer of it. Violating its laws, he ceases to belong to it, and indeed fights against it. The survival of the state and his own cannot then go together, and one or the other has to be destroyed. When the guilty man is executed, he dies less as a citizen than as an enemy. His prosecution and verdict show and declare that he has violated the social compact, and therefore is no longer a member of the state. By residing there he had at least professed to be a member. He must therefore be removed, through banishment for breaking the compact, or through death if he is to be treated as a public enemy. An enemy of this kind is no moral person; he is a mere individual, and it is precisely in this case that the right of war allows the vanquished to be killed.

One might object that sentencing a criminal is a particular act. It is; and for that reason it does not belong to the sovereign itself. Supreme power may delegate the authority to carry it out, though it cannot exercise that authority directly. My ideas on this point fit together, even if I cannot explain them all at once.

We should also notice that executions carried out often are always evidence of a weak or careless government. No criminal is beyond all useful purpose. No one should be put to death, even as an example, unless the community cannot be protected from danger while he lives.

Pardon, meaning exemption of a guilty man from the penalty set by law and imposed by the judge, belongs solely to the authority above both judge and law, which is the sovereign. Even then its right in the matter is far from clear, and the occasions for exercising it are few. In a well-governed state punishments are rare, not because many are forgiven but because few commit crimes; when the state is failing, the multitude of crimes secures impunity for them. The Roman republic never saw the senate or the consuls attempt pardons, nor the people either, even though the people sometimes reversed their own sentences. Frequent pardons announce that crimes will soon have no need of them, and everyone can see where that road leads. Yet something in me resists, and my pen stops here. Whoever has never done wrong, and so has never required mercy, is the proper person to pursue these questions further.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. VI. On the law.
paragraphs: Once the social compact has brought the body politic into being and given it life, we must now provide it with action and will by establishing a legislature. The founding act that creates this body has not yet settled what it needs in order to survive.

Whatever is good and orderly is so by the nature of things, whatever men may have agreed. Justice has its single source in God; if only we knew how to take it from that height, government and laws would be unnecessary. A universal justice does exist, born of reason alone, but to be accepted among us it must be reciprocal. Judged by human standards, the laws of justice are pointless among men because they lack natural sanction; they profit the wicked and hurt the just, who observes them toward everybody while nobody observes them toward him. We therefore need conventions and laws to connect obligations with entitlements and to direct justice toward its proper end. In the natural state, where all things are held jointly, I owe nothing to people I have promised nothing, and I acknowledge as another's only what I have no use for myself. Under civil society the position differs, since there every right is determined by law.

At last we must ask what a law is. So long as the only meaning we give to the word is a metaphysical one, we will keep talking at cross purposes; and even after explaining what natural law is, we will be no wiser about the law of a state. I have already argued that a general will cannot concern a particular object. Any such object must be either within the state or beyond it. If beyond, a will belonging to others is not general with respect to it. If within, it is a piece of the state, and between the whole and the piece a relationship exists which creates two distinct beings: the piece, and the whole with that piece taken away. But the whole minus one part is no longer the whole; as long as the relation continues, there is no whole at all, only two unequal parts. So the will of either one cannot be general in relation to the other.

When an entire people makes a decision about the entire people, it considers only the body as a whole. If any relation is formed, it is between the complete object viewed in one way and that same complete object viewed in another, with no part cut away. The subject of the decision is thus as general as the will making it. This is the act I call a law.

When I say laws always have a general object, I mean that a law deals with its subjects collectively and with their actions in the abstract; it never concerns an individual or a particular deed. The law may grant kinds of privilege, but cannot award one to a named person. It may create classes of citizens and define the qualifications for membership, but cannot choose the people admitted to them. It may establish a lawful form of government and hereditary succession, but cannot select a king or name the royal family. In short, no duty concerning an individual object belongs to the legislative authority.

Once we see this, it is immediately clear how senseless it is to ask who has power to make laws, since laws are acts of the general will; or whether a prince stands above the laws, since he is only one member of the state. It also becomes clear that a law cannot be unjust: nothing can be unjust to itself. We can also understand how someone can be free while subject to laws, because those laws simply record our own will.

It is also clear that a law joins the universal character of the will to the universal character of its object. Whatever any individual, whatever his rank, orders on his own authority cannot therefore be a law. Even a command issued by supreme power about a particular matter is only a decree, not a law; it is an act of government, not an act of sovereignty.

I therefore call every state ruled by laws a republic, whatever its administrative form. Only there does the public interest govern, and whatever is public has substance. Every lawful government is republican. I will explain later what I mean by government.

By “republican” I do not mean specifically aristocracy or democracy. I mean any government guided by the people’s general will, which is expressed as law. A government need not be merged with the sovereign to be lawful; it must serve as the sovereign’s minister. In this sense even a monarchy is a republic. I will explain this more fully in the next book.

Laws are, properly speaking, nothing more than the terms of civil association. The people subject to the laws should be their authors, since it is for the associates alone to settle the terms of their association. But how are they to settle them? Will they do it by unanimous consent, or by a flash of insight? Is there any means by which the political body can voice what it wants? Who will give it the foresight needed to frame its enactments and publish them in advance, or how will it announce them in a crisis? And how could a crowd without understanding, frequently ignorant of its own wishes because it seldom grasps where its good lies, carry through a task so vast and arduous as the creation of a code of laws? Left to itself, a people always desires the good but does not always perceive it. The general will is always right; the judgment which directs it is not always well instructed. Things have to be presented to the people as they are, and at times as they ought to seem; shown the right road they are looking for; protected against the pull of particular wills; helped to grasp matters of place and time; and taught to weigh the attraction of present, visible advantages against the danger of far-off, concealed evils. Private persons perceive the good and turn it down; the public desires the good yet cannot perceive it. Each needs a guide. Individuals must be pressed to bring their inclinations into agreement with reason, while the public must be instructed in what it actually wants. When the public is enlightened in this way, understanding and will become one in the social body, its parts work in complete harmony, and the whole finally attains its maximum strength. From this arises the need for a legislator.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. VII. Of the genius and character of a legislator.
paragraphs: To discover the social arrangements best suited to nations would take an intelligence beyond ordinary human reach: one able to witness every human passion without feeling any itself, wholly unconnected to human nature yet perfectly acquainted with it, and whose happiness did not depend on ours but which would still devote itself to our welfare. Making laws for human beings is truly a task for the gods.
Nations become celebrated only after their institutions have begun to decline. Lycurgus’s laws kept the Spartans content for generations before Greece heard of their fame.

Caligula’s argument is used as a practical claim, while Plato himself uses the same reasoning as a matter of principle when he describes the civil or royal person in his account of kings. Yet if a great prince is rare, how much rarer must a great legislator be? The prince need only follow the design the legislator has laid out. One is the inventive mind that designs the machine; the other is merely the worker who assembles it. As Montesquieu says, at the beginning of republics their leading citizens shape the institutions, and later those institutions shape the republic’s leaders.

Anyone who undertakes to shape a political community must believe himself capable of changing human nature completely: turning each person, previously solitary and self-reliant, into a part of a larger whole from which he will in one sense receive his life and being. He must be able to reshape the human constitution and strengthen it, replacing a person’s separate physical existence with a partial moral one. In short, he must take away natural abilities and give people new powers they cannot use without one another’s help. The more natural strength is diminished and extinguished, the greater and more lasting the acquired strength becomes, and the more complete and firm the social institution. If every citizen can accomplish nothing alone and depends on all the others, while the strength gained by the body as a whole equals or exceeds the combined natural powers of its members, the legislature has reached the highest perfection available to it Citizens gain this moral existence by taking part in a common public life.

In every respect, the legislator is an exceptional figure in the state. His genius makes him extraordinary, but so does his role. He is neither magistrate nor sovereign. His function, which establishes the republic, does not form part of its constitution. It is instead a special and superior task, separate from the work of government. If the person who commands citizens must not also control the laws, then the person who controls laws must likewise not command citizens. Otherwise he could make laws serve his own passions and use them to prolong injustice; he could never stop private aims from distorting the whole system altogether.

At the time Lycurgus gave his country its laws, the first thing he did was resign the throne. Most Greek cities customarily gave outsiders the task of drawing up their laws. Italy's modern republics often followed this custom, and Geneva did likewise, to good effect. In its finest period, Rome saw all the crimes of tyranny arise again within it and nearly perished, because legislative authority and sovereign power had been put in the same hands.

People who know Calvin only as a theologian understand little of his wide-ranging talent. The legal code in which he played a substantial part honours him as much as his religious system. Whatever changes time may bring to our public worship, this great man’s memory will remain respected for as long as patriotism and a sense of liberty endure.

Even the decemvirs never claimed the right to enact laws by their own authority alone. “Nothing we propose,” they told the people, “can become law without your approval. Romans, make yourselves the authors of the laws on which your happiness rests.”

The legislator who drafts laws, then, has no right to declare them binding as laws; nor can the people, even if they wished, strip themselves of this right, which cannot be handed away. Under the fundamental compact, only the general will binds individuals, and there is no way to know whether a particular will agrees with it until the people freely vote on it. I have made this point already, though repeating it may not have been needless.
Thus lawmaking brings together two things that seem impossible to reconcile: a design beyond human ability, carried out by an authority that has no power.

A further difficulty needs mention. Wise men who try to address ordinary people in the language of the wise will not be understood. Yet there are countless ideas that cannot be rendered in popular speech. Perspectives that are too general, and aims that are too remote, lie equally outside the common range of understanding. Since each individual approves only the government that serves his own private interest, he can hardly see what advantages he is to gain from the constant sacrifices that good laws demand. For a newly formed people to come to value healthy political maxims and keep to the rules of statecraft, cause and effect would have to change places. The communal spirit that ought to come out of the institution would have to guide the act of founding it, and people would need to be already, before any laws exist, what the laws are to turn them into. Since the lawgiver can employ neither force nor reasoning, he has to turn to a different order of authority, one that can win assent without demonstrating anything and constrain without using violence. That is why, in every age, the founders of nations have been driven to bring in heaven and to ascribe their own wisdom to the gods, so that the peoples might obey state laws as they obey natural ones, seeing one and the same power behind the creation of the city and the creation of mankind, and so accept freely, and without resistance, the burden of the public good.

The lawgiver puts into the mouths of the immortals the decisions of that exalted reason which soars beyond the understanding of ordinary men, so that divine authority may carry along those whom human prudence could not stir. But not every man is able to make the gods speak, or to be believed when he gives himself out as their spokesman. What truly certifies the lawgiver's mission is the miracle of his own towering mind. Anybody can chisel tablets, pay off a priestess of an oracle, boast of private conversations with a deity, teach a bird to murmur in his ear, or hit on some other coarse trick for gulling a nation. A man who knows nothing beyond such devices may by chance collect a band of fools around him, yet he will never establish an empire, and his reckless construction will shortly collapse together with him. Empty deceits form only a fleeting bond; only wisdom makes it lasting. Jewish law endures to this day, and so does the code of Ishmael's descendant, which has ruled half the globe for a thousand years; both still testify to the stature of those who drew them up. Vain philosophy and blind party spirit see them as mere fortunate impostors, but the real statesman wonders in their institutions at the mighty and far-seeing mind that lies behind every lasting foundation.

None of this proves, as Warburton claims, that religion and government share one purpose in our own times. It shows only that, when societies were first founded, religion was used to assist government.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. VIII. Of the people.
paragraphs: Before an architect puts up a building, he surveys and tests the ground to see whether it can carry the weight of the structure. In the same way, a wise lawgiver does not start by drawing up good laws; he first investigates whether the people they are meant for are able to endure them. This is why Plato declined to legislate for the Arcadians and the Cyrenians: he knew they were rich and given to luxury, and would not tolerate equality. This is why Crete had fine laws and wicked inhabitants: Minos had set himself to rule a people already steeped in vice. Many nations have shone brilliantly on the earth without ever being able to bear good laws, and even those who could bear them did so only for a short season. Peoples, like persons, are teachable only while young, and become impossible to correct as they age. Once habits are fixed and prejudices have taken root, trying to reform them is a risky and hopeless undertaking. A people will not even let anyone touch its sores in order to heal them, like those faint-hearted invalids who tremble at the sight of the doctor. Still, just as certain illnesses disturb the mind and wipe out memory of the past, so states sometimes pass through violent upheavals that do the same to a people: dread of what happened takes the place of forgetting, and the nation, scorched and drained by civil war, rises again, so to speak, from its own ashes and recovers the vigour of youth as it escapes the grip of death. That was Sparta's case in Lycurgus's day and Rome's once the Tarquins were gone; in recent times it was the case for Holland and for Switzerland when their tyrants were expelled. Yet such episodes seldom occur. They are exceptions, each explained by something peculiar to the constitution of the state in which it happened. Nor can a people experience one twice. It may recover freedom while it is still rough and uncultivated, but not after the vital resources of civil life have been exhausted. Then disorder may destroy it, but revolutions cannot rebuild its liberty; it needs a master from then on, not a liberator. Let every free nation therefore keep this rule in mind: liberty can be gained, but once lost it can never be recovered.

Peoples, like individuals, have a period of maturity that should come before laws are imposed on them. It is not always easy to identify that moment, and getting ahead of it can be dangerous. One people may be ready for discipline in childhood; another may need centuries before it can accept restraint. The Russians, for example, will never become truly refined because they were disciplined too early. Peter could imitate, but he lacked the creative genius that brings new things into being. Some of his measures were sound enough, yet most came at the wrong time or in the wrong place. He saw that his subjects were barbarians, but failed to see that they were not ready to become polished. He tried to civilize them when he should merely have restrained their brutality. He wanted to turn them at once into Germans and Englishmen, when he ought first to have made them Russians. In this way he stopped them from becoming what they otherwise might have been, convincing them they were already something else. A French tutor similarly trains a pupil to make a display in childhood and then never make one again. Russia, while striving to bring all Europe under its control, will itself be subdued. Its Tartar neighbours will one day become masters of Russia and of us. This seems inevitable to me, since all Europe’s monarchs appear to be working together to hasten that upheaval.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. IX. The subject continued.
paragraphs: Nature sets limits to the size of a well-proportioned human body; beyond them she produces only giants or dwarfs. The body politic likewise has boundaries within which it should be kept, so that it is neither too large to govern well nor too small to maintain its independence. Every political body has a maximum strength it cannot surpass, and often loses strength when it extends its rule. The wider the social bond reaches, the looser it becomes. In general, a small state is proportionately stronger than a great one.

A thousand reasons could support this rule. First, governing becomes harder the farther one moves from the seat of government, just as a body’s weight is greatest at the far end of a long lever. Government also grows more burdensome as it is divided into layers. Each town pays for its own local administration; each district’s costs are then paid by the same people, followed by those of the province, then of regional governments and their viceroys. Every level must be paid in proportion to its rank, always at the expense of the unhappy population. Finally the highest administration crushes the people under the full weight of its oppression. All these needless expenses must steadily impoverish them. The many levels of authority do not govern them better than a single order of rulers would. Yet despite having so many officials, the state has no proper resources for an emergency; when one comes, it is already close to ruin That recurring drain leaves little room for useful public spending.

Nor is this the only problem. Government becomes less energetic in enforcing laws, removing private abuses, correcting wrongs, or preventing distant provinces from plotting rebellion. The people feel less attachment to their leaders, whom they never see; to their country, which seems to them as large as the whole world; and to their fellow citizens, most of whom are strangers. One set of laws cannot suit so many different peoples, customs, and climates, or make all equally content under the same government. Yet different laws create difficulty and confusion among people who share one administration and are constantly in contact: they move between homes, marry across regions, and, raised under different customs, can hardly know when their property is safe. Great talents stay hidden, virtue goes unnoticed, and vice thrives without punishment in the crowd of strangers around the capital. The leaders, buried in business, cannot look into matters themselves, and leave the state’s government to deputies and clerks. In the end, keeping general authority over distant officials, who are always ready to encroach or impose their own will, consumes public attention. Nothing remains for the people’s happiness, and scarcely anything for their defence in an emergency. A body too unwieldy for its constitution loses strength and sinks beneath its own weight.

On the other hand, a state needs a firm foundation. It must be solid enough to withstand the shocks it will inevitably face and to make the efforts needed to keep its independence. Nations all have a kind of outward-driving force, continually pressing against one another and seeking, like Descartes’s vortices, to enlarge themselves at their neighbours’ cost. The weak therefore risk being swallowed by the strong. Their only security is to remain in balance with the others, with equal pressure on every side and political resistance.

We can see, then, that a state should sometimes widen its boundaries and sometimes limit them.
