One of the chief skills of civil policy is to tell these cases apart and set the proportion most helpful to preserving the state. As a general rule, reasons for expansion concern external and relative matters, and must yield to reasons for contraction, which concern internal and absolute matters. A sound, vigorous constitution comes first. A good government deserves far more trust than the resources an extensive territory might supply within the country’s own political life in civic life.

This is not to deny that some states have been formed so that conquest was essential to their very constitution. They may even have congratulated themselves on this fortunate necessity, which nevertheless marked, at the height of their greatness, the unavoidable moment of their fall.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. X. The subject continued.
paragraphs: There are two ways to gauge a body politic: by how much land it covers and by how many people it holds. A fitting balance between the two is what gives the state its true greatness. People constitute the state, and the soil nourishes the people; the right balance is therefore reached when the land is enough to maintain its inhabitants and the inhabitants are as numerous as the land can maintain. In that proportion lies the greatest strength of a given number of people. If there is too much land, defending it is a burden, working it is inadequate, and its yield is surplus; hence defensive wars have their immediate cause. If there is too little, the state is compelled to rely on its neighbours for part of its sustenance; hence offensive wars have theirs. A nation whose position leaves it nothing but trade or warfare is inevitably weak. It relies on its neighbours and on chance, and can have only a brief and precarious existence. It must either conquer and so alter its position, or be conquered and be reduced to nothing. Its independence can be kept only by being tiny or enormous.

It is difficult to calculate the exact balance between the amount of land and the population it can support. Soil varies in quality, fertility, and what it produces; climate also matters. The people differ just as much in their habits and physical needs: some consume little on fertile ground, while others need a great deal from barren land. We must also consider how readily women bear children, what circumstances increase or reduce population, and how many newcomers the legislator might attract through the benefits offered by his government. He should therefore judge not by the population now present but by what he can foresee in the future—not by today’s number but by the growth that will naturally follow. A thousand local conditions may allow a state to hold more land than it seems to need at present. A people might spread across a wide mountainous region, where forests and pastures take less work than cultivated fields; experience also tells us that women have more children there than on level ground. A large sloping surface may have only a small horizontal base, and it is by that base alone that we should estimate how much land can grow crops. By contrast, a people may live in a much smaller area along the sea, or among rocks and nearly barren sand, because fishing supplies their food in place of agriculture. They can also relieve their community of excess population by sending out colonies. Finally, they need to live close together to repel pirate attacks in that setting.

To the conditions already mentioned for establishing a people, we must add one that nothing else can supply and without which every other condition is pointless: they must have peace and plenty. The period when a state is being formed is like the time when soldiers are first arranged into a battalion: they are then least able to resist and easiest to defeat. Afterward, even when in complete disorder, they would resist more strongly than during that first unsettled moment, when each person is more occupied with his own place than with the shared danger. If war, famine, or rebellion broke out at this critical stage, the state would certainly be overthrown.

There have indeed been governments founded in times of disorder, but those governments themselves destroyed the state. Usurpers always cause or choose such troubled times to pass, in the midst of general alarm, ruinous laws that the people would never adopt with a cool head. The choice of the moment for legislation is one of the surest marks by which one can tell the work of a lawgiver from that of a tyrant.

If we ask which people are ready to receive a system of laws, I would answer: those already joined by some original bond of interest or agreement, yet not truly subject to regular laws; those whose customs and prejudices have not taken deep root; those who need not fear being suddenly swallowed by an invasion and who can meet each neighbour separately without joining their quarrels, or call on one to help resist another. They should be people whose members know one another, among whom no one has to be burdened beyond what he can bear; who can survive without other nations and whose absence no other nation could not survive. They should be neither wealthy nor destitute, but self-sufficient. In a word, they should combine the steadiness of an old nation with the readiness to learn of a new one. The hardest part of legislation is less knowing what to establish than knowing what to remove. Its rare failures also reflect how impossible it is to find nature’s simplicity within society’s many demands. These conditions seldom come together, which is why so few states have much to praise in their constitutions. There is still one European country fit to receive laws: the island of Corsica. The bravery and determination with which its people won back and defended their liberty should inspire some wise person to teach them how to preserve it. I cannot help thinking that this small island may one day astonish Europe.

If two neighbouring peoples were placed so that one could not survive without the other, the first would be in a very harsh position and the second in great danger. Any wise nation in that position would free itself from the dependence as quickly as possible. The republic of Tlaxcala, in the middle of the Mexican empire, preferred to go without salt rather than buy it from the Mexicans or accept it as a gift. Its prudent citizens saw through the trap concealed in such generosity. That is how they kept their freedom. This little state, surrounded by the vast empire, ultimately helped bring about its downfall.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. XI. Of the various systems of legislature.
paragraphs: If we ask what the greatest good consists of, or what every system of lawmaking should aim to achieve, the answer comes down to two main ends: liberty and equality. Liberty is needed because every dependence on a private person drains strength from the state as a whole; equality is needed because liberty cannot survive without it.

I have already explained what social liberty is. Equality does not mean that everyone must have exactly the same wealth or power. It means that power must never be used against good order and law, and that no citizen should be rich enough to buy another or so poor that he must sell himself. This requires restraint in the wealth and influence of the great, and restraint in the wants and greed of those with less Such restraint also limits the dependence that unequal wealth creates.

If you want to give a state strength and stability, keep the two extremes as far apart as possible: let there be neither rich people nor beggars. These conditions go together, and both damage the commonwealth. One creates tyrants, the other those who support tyranny. Through them public liberty is traded: some buy it and others sell it.

People say this kind of equality is only an abstract fantasy and cannot be put into practice. But even if abuses cannot be avoided, does that mean we should not correct them? Things continually work against equality; for that very reason, laws should be designed to protect it.

These general aims of legislation must be adjusted to each country’s location, the character of its people, and the other circumstances that call for a distinct system of laws. The best system in theory may not be the one best suited to a particular state. If, for example, the soil is barren or the country too small for its population, encourage crafts and industry, whose products can be traded for what the people need. But if there are fertile hills and productive valleys, a rich soil and too few inhabitants, turn to farming, which supports population, and drive out destructive arts that gather the few people into one or two places and leave the rest of the country empty. If your country has a broad, convenient coastline, fill the sea with ships and cultivate navigation and trade; these may bring a brilliant but brief period of prosperity. If instead the waves break their force against your inaccessible cliffs, remain uncultivated and unlearned; perhaps you will live more comfortably, more virtuously, and certainly more happily. Beyond principles shared by all nations, each people has its own particular influence that makes its own laws suitable to itself alone. In ancient times among the Hebrews, and in more recent times among the Arabs, religion was the main concern of the nation; for Athens it was learning, for Carthage and Tyre commerce, for Rhodes seafaring, for Sparta war, and for Rome public virtue. The author of *The Spirit of Laws* has shown through many examples how a lawgiver should shape a system to serve each of these ends.

The Marquis d’A. says that the benefit of foreign trade is an illusion for the kingdom as a whole. It may enrich a few people, and perhaps some cities, but the nation gains nothing and the people are no better off.

A state’s constitution becomes truly solid and lasting when its natural and social relations agree. Then legislation works with nature, and laws merely confirm and, as it were, correct what nature dictates. But if the legislator misunderstands his aim and chooses a principle at odds with the nature of things—if law directs people towards slavery while nature favours freedom, towards riches while nature supports population, or towards peace while nature leads to war and conquest—the laws will gradually lose their force. The constitution will change, and the state will remain unsettled until it is wholly transformed or destroyed and nature has taken control again.

chapters.title: Book II. CHAP. XII. On the division of the laws.
paragraphs: To arrange the government of the whole and give the constitution the best possible form, several considerations must be weighed. The first is how the whole body acts on itself, that is, the relation of the whole to the whole, or of the sovereign to the state, a relation made up of the relations between intermediate terms, as will be shown later on.

Laws governing this relation are called political laws, and also fundamental laws—rightly so when they are wisely established. If a state has only one good method of government, the people fortunate enough to have found it should keep to that method. But why should a people regard bad or defective laws as fundamental? Besides, a nation remains free to change even its best laws whenever it wishes. If people want to harm themselves, who has the right to stop them in their present arrangement in that case.

The second relation is between the members of the community and one another, and between each of them and the whole body. The first relation should be as small as possible, the second as large as possible, so that every citizen is as independent of everyone else as can be, and as dependent on the city as possible. Both results come from the same means: only the state’s power can secure the liberty of its members. This second kind of relation is the immediate basis of civil laws.

We may also consider a third relation, between an individual and the law, which gives rise directly to penal laws. In truth, however, these form less a separate class than the means by which all the other laws are enforced.

To these three kinds we can add a fourth, more important than all the others. It is written neither in bronze nor marble, but in the hearts of the citizens, and forms the state’s true constitution. These laws gain influence day by day. When other laws grow old and obsolete, they give them fresh life and strength. They preserve in the people’s hearts the original spirit of the institution and gradually replace authority with the force of habit. I mean manners, customs, and above all public opinion. Modern politicians ignore or dismiss them, yet the success of every other law depends on them. These are the matters on which a true lawgiver works quietly, while seeming to limit himself to specific rules. Those rules are only the central support of a vaulted roof; manners develop more slowly, but eventually form its firm and lasting arch.
Of these classes, only political laws, which establish the form of government, relate to my present subject.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. I. On government in general.
paragraphs: Before discussing the various forms of government, we should first settle exactly what the word means. It has not yet been clearly explained This definition matters.
I must first warn the reader to study this chapter with great care. I cannot make myself clear to anyone who does not give it close attention.

Every free action has two causes working together: one moral, the will that decides on the action, and one physical, the power that carries it out. If I walk towards a particular place, I must first want to go, and then my feet must move me forward. A paralyzed person may want to run while a strong runner may refuse; in either case, the lack of power or lack of will has the same result, and the person stays where he is. The body politic moves by these same two principles, which are likewise distinguished as power and will. The will is called legislative power, and the power is called executive power. Nothing is or should be done unless both take part.

We have seen already that legislative power rests with the people as a whole and can rest with no one else. From the principles laid down, it is equally easy to infer that executive power cannot belong to the people at large in their role as lawmaker or sovereign. For that power works only through particular acts, and such acts are outside the province of law, and therefore outside that of the sovereign, whose acts can never be anything but laws.

Public force must therefore be attached to a suitable agent who can bring it together and set it in motion according to the general will. This agent connects state and sovereign and serves the same purpose in the political body as the union of soul and body in a human being. This explains the nature of government, so often confused with the sovereign even though government is only its instrument.

What, then, is government? It is an intermediate body, set between subjects and sovereign to connect them with one another. It is charged with carrying out the laws and preserving civil and political liberty.

The persons who make up this body are called magistrates or kings, meaning governors, and the body as a whole is called the prince. Those who say that the act by which a people submits to its leaders is not a contract are therefore quite right. It is nothing more than a commission given to those leaders, an office in which they serve as simple officials of the sovereign, using in its name the power it has entrusted to them, a power it can restrict, alter, or take back whenever it wishes; for to give up the right to do so would be contrary to the very nature of society and of its being.
Thus in Venice the senate’s college is called the most serene prince, even when the doge is absent.
I call the lawful exercise of executive power “government” or “supreme administration.” I call the person or body charged with that administration the prince or magistrate.

The government is where those intermediate forces are found, whose mutual relations add up to the relation between the whole and the whole, which is to say between sovereign and state. This last relation may be pictured as that between the outer terms of a continuous proportion, with the government as its middle term. From the sovereign the government takes the orders that it passes on to the people. To keep the state properly in balance, all things considered, there must be an equivalence between the momentum or strength of the government in itself and the momentum or strength of the citizens, who are sovereign in one respect, collectively, and subjects in another, individually.

If any of these three terms changes, the proportions are immediately destroyed. If the sovereign tries to govern directly, if the magistrate makes laws, or if the subjects refuse obedience, disorder follows. Will and power no longer work together, the state breaks apart, and despotism or anarchy takes its place. Moreover, there can be only one middle term for any given relation, so each state can have only one best form of government. Yet a thousand events can change the relations among a people. Different governments may therefore suit different peoples, and even the same people at different times.
To give an idea of the different relations possible between these two extremes, I will use population as an example because it is easiest to express It is easy to overlook.

Suppose a state contains ten thousand citizens. The sovereign must be considered collectively, as one body, while each person as a subject is considered individually. The ratio of sovereign to subject is therefore ten thousand to one. Each member shares only one ten-thousandth of sovereign authority, while his whole person is subject to it. If the population grows to one hundred thousand, each subject remains just as fully subject to the laws, but his share in sovereignty and his vote in making those laws shrink to one hundred-thousandth—ten times smaller than before. The subject always counts as one whole individual, while the sovereign side grows with the citizenry. The larger the state becomes, the more the subject’s liberty diminishes The comparison also shows why political membership gives each person a smaller share of collective rule as the body grows, even though law continues to bind each person completely.

When I say the proportion grows, I mean it moves farther from equality. In the language of geometry, a ratio that grows larger is, in ordinary speech, considered smaller. In the first usage we measure the relation by its extent; in the second, we judge it by how close the two terms are to being alike.

The smaller each private vote is in relation to the collective voice—in other words, the smaller the force of custom is beside the law—the more the general power that restrains the people must be increased. Government therefore needs relatively greater strength as the population grows.

On the other hand, the greater size of a state gives those entrusted with public authority more chances and temptations to misuse their power. So the more force government has to restrain the people, the more strength the sovereign in turn needs to restrain government. I am not speaking here of absolute power, but of the relative strength of the parts that make up the state.

These two relations show that the fixed proportion among sovereign, prince, and people is no arbitrary invention. It follows necessarily from the political body’s very existence. The people as subjects form one fixed term, represented by unity. Whenever the combined ratio grows or shrinks, the simple ratio must change in the same way, and the middle term changes with it. There is therefore no single permanent constitution for government: there can be as many kinds of government as there are states of different sizes across the whole population.

If someone mocks my system and says that, to find this middle term and arrange government properly, we need only calculate the square root of the population, I answer that I use population only as an example. The relations I mean are measured not only by the number of individuals but, more generally, by the quantity of action produced by several combined causes. I borrow geometrical terms for brevity, but I know that exact mathematical precision cannot be expected in a discussion of moral quantities This middle office remains distinct from both sides for the administrative structure to work.

Government, on a small scale, resembles the larger political body that contains it. It is a moral person with particular capacities: active as the sovereign and passive as the state. It can itself be divided into other observable relations, creating one proportional scale and then another within it, as we move through the ranks of courts, until we reach the smallest indivisible term: the one chief or supreme magistrate. He can be pictured at the centre of the progression, as a unit between a series of fractions and a series of whole numbers.
Rather than burden the reader with a heap of terms, we will simply regard the government as a new body inside the state, separate from both the people and the sovereign, and standing between them.

There is, however, one essential difference between government and the state. The state exists in its own right; government exists only through the sovereign. The prince’s ruling will is—or ought to be—only the general will, in other words the law. The prince’s power is only the public power concentrated in his hands. If he tries to act with absolute authority of his own, he damages the union of the whole. If at last the prince develops a private will more active than the sovereign’s and uses the public power entrusted to him to force obedience to that private will, there will in effect be two sovereigns, one lawful and one actual. The social bond immediately disappears, and the political body is dissolved.

For the government body to exist with a life of its own, distinct from that of the state, and for its members to work together towards the purpose for which it was created, it needs a particular identity and a shared sensibility, along with a will and power of its own to preserve itself. Such a separate existence requires assemblies and councils, a power to debate and decide, and rights, titles, and privileges belonging specifically to the prince. The more demanding a magistrate’s position, the more honourable it must be. The difficulty is to arrange all the subordinate parts of government so that it can strengthen its own structure without harming the state’s. It must also keep its own strength, meant to preserve government, distinct from public force, meant to preserve the state. In a word, it must always be ready to sacrifice government for the people, never the people for government in every part of its public work.

We may add that, although this artificial body of government is created by another artificial body, and has only a borrowed, subordinate existence, it can still act with varying degrees of energy and speed. It can be healthier or weaker, so to speak. It can depart from the purpose for which it was established to a greater or lesser degree without directly opposing that purpose, depending on how it is organized.

All these differences produce the various relations and proportions that government should have to the state, depending on the particular circumstances that shape it. A government that is best in itself may often become the worst if its parts are not adjusted to the weaknesses of the political body it serves.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. II. On the principle which constitutes the different forms of government.
paragraphs: To explain the general reason for these differences, we must distinguish prince from government, just as I earlier distinguished sovereign from state. The magistracy may contain many members or only a few. We have also seen that the relation of sovereign to subject grows as the population grows. By an obvious parallel, the same is true of the relation between government and its magistrates as parts of one political arrangement.

The government’s total force always equals the force of the state and does not change. It follows that the more this force is divided among the members of government, the less can be applied to the people as a whole.
A government placed in the hands of the largest number of magistrates must therefore be the weakest. This is a basic principle, so we should take care to explain it.

Three essentially different wills can be told apart in the person of a magistrate. First there is his own particular will, which looks only to his private advantage. Second is the will common to the magistrates, which looks solely to the advantage of the prince; toward the government this will is a general one, whereas toward the state, which the government makes up only a section of, it is a particular one. Third is the people's will, the will of the sovereign, which is general toward the state taken as a whole and also toward the government taken as one piece of that whole.

In a well-designed system of laws, a person’s private will should count for nothing; the will of the government as a body should be sharply limited; and the general or sovereign will should rule and direct all the others alone.

Nature, however, arranges these wills in the reverse order: the more concentrated a will is within itself, the more active it becomes. The general will is weakest, the government’s will next, and each individual’s will strongest. Every member of the administration should therefore be considered first as an individual, next as a magistrate, and last as a citizen—the exact reverse of society’s required order in the community.

With that settled, suppose the administration of government is entrusted to one person. His individual will and the will of the magistracy are then completely joined, so the latter gains the greatest intensity. Since the use of force depends on the strength of the will, and the government’s total force never changes, the administration of one person must be the most active of all in this model of administration.

Now imagine joining execution to lawmaking, making the prince sovereign, and turning all citizens into officers. The administration’s intention would be confused with the common will but gain no further activity, while each person’s private aim could act at full strength. Total power would stay the same, yet government’s effective force relative to the whole would be at its lowest.

These relations are certain and can be supported in other ways. A magistrate acts more actively in that role than a citizen acts in his. The individual’s private will must therefore have a larger influence in government administration than it has in sovereign decisions: nearly every magistrate has some governmental duty, whereas no citizen as a private person performs any act of sovereignty. Also, a state’s actual force grows as its size grows, though not always in direct proportion. But while the state remains the same, adding more magistrates is useless: it gives government no extra strength, since its force is always the state’s force and therefore remains constant. The government’s relative strength and activity diminish even though its total strength does not increase of the same state.

It is also clear that public business moves faster or slower depending on how many people are charged with handling it. Excessive caution leaves too little to chance; opportunities for success are often lost, and deliberation itself can defeat its own purpose under public authority in practice.

This shows that the reins of government loosen as the number of magistrates grows. I have already shown that the restraining power of government must increase as the population grows. The number of magistrates should therefore stand in inverse proportion to the relation between subjects and sovereign: the larger the state, the more concentrated its government should be, and the number of leaders should fall as the people’s number rises as the nation grows.

My remarks here concern the relative strength of the government, not whether it is right or fitting. For on the other side it is certain that the larger the body of magistrates, the closer the will of that body comes to the general will of the whole people, whereas under a single ruler the will of the magistracy is, as I said before, no more than one man's. What is gained in one respect is thus lost in the other, and the lawgiver's craft lies in finding the fixed point at which the government's strength and its will, always inversely proportioned, meet in the ratio that serves the state best.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. III. Of the actual distinctions of governments.
paragraphs: The previous chapter explained why we distinguish kinds and forms of government by the number of people who make them up. We must now see how these distinctions work in practice.

First, the sovereign authority may entrust government to the whole people or to most of them, so that there are more magistrates than private citizens. This form is called democracy chosen from among the citizens themselves eligible.
Or supreme power may place government in the hands of a small number, leaving more private citizens than magistrates. This form is called aristocracy in the body of public officials.
Or government may be entrusted to a single magistrate, who passes some of his authority on to everyone else. This third form, the most common one, is called monarchy or royal government.

Note that all these forms, especially the first two, admit various degrees of perfection and quite a wide range of variation. A democracy may take in the whole people or be confined to half of it. An aristocracy can range in size from half the people to a tiny handful. Even monarchy can be divided up to some extent. Sparta, for example, by its constitution always had two kings, and Rome at one time had as many as eight emperors without the empire being truly split. So there is a point at which every form of government merges into the one nearest to it, and under only three headings government can in fact take as many different shapes as the state has citizens.

Going further, a single government can be split into several parts, each with a different administration. Their combinations can produce many other forms, and each of these can be multiplied again by every simple form that can be mixed in turn when combined.
Politicians throughout history have argued about which kind of government is best without considering that any one form may be best in some situations and worst in others.

If the number of chief magistrates in different states varies inversely with the number of citizens, then democracy is generally better suited to small states, aristocracy to those of medium size, and monarchy to large states. This rule follows directly from the principles we have laid down, though it is impossible to list all the many circumstances that might create exceptions.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. IV. Of a Democracy.
paragraphs: Surely the person who makes a law should understand better than anyone else how it ought to be interpreted and carried out. It might therefore seem that the best constitution would place both lawmaking and execution in the same hands. But that very arrangement makes the government imperfect, because it removes the necessary distinction between its parts. Prince and sovereign become one and the same person, producing what I might call government with no government at all.

The same power should not make laws and execute them, and the people as a whole should not have their attention drawn from general questions to particular affairs. Nothing is more dangerous than private interests influencing public business. It is less harmful for government to misuse the laws than for the legislature to become corrupt; that corruption is inevitable when private aims direct its work. In that case the state is fundamentally changed, and reform becomes impossible. A people that would not abuse its governing power would be no more likely to abuse its independence; and a people that always governed well would have no need of government.

If we use the word in its strictest sense, a genuine democracy has never existed and never will exist. It runs against the natural order for most of the people to govern and the rest to be governed. It is impossible to imagine the entire people staying personally assembled to manage public affairs. As soon as they appoint deputies or representatives, the form of administration changes.

We may take this as a rule: when the duties of government are divided among several bodies, the one with the fewest members will sooner or later become the most powerful, if for no other reason than that it can get things done more quickly.

Such a form of government also depends on many conditions that rarely occur together. First, the state must be small enough that people can assemble easily and all know one another personally. Second, their way of life must be simple enough to keep public business from becoming complicated or too tangled to discuss. Third, people’s rank and wealth must be fairly equal, or equality in rights and authority cannot last. Finally, there must be little or no luxury. Luxury either comes from wealth or makes wealth necessary; it corrupts rich and poor alike, the first through what they possess and the second through what they lack. It exchanges love of country for idleness and vanity, deprives the state of its citizens by making them dependent on one another and by subjecting everyone to public prejudice in public decisions.

This explains why a celebrated writer made virtue the first principle of republican government: these conditions cannot all exist without public virtue. But this great thinker often fell into error and imprecision by failing to distinguish properly among cases. He did not see that sovereign authority is everywhere the same, so the same principle must apply in every well-ordered state, though in differing degrees according to its form of government in the state.

No form is more exposed to civil war and internal upheaval than democracy or popular government. None is so constantly inclined to change, or requires so much vigilance and courage to keep it from changing. In this constitution especially, citizens must always remain ready to defend themselves and sincerely repeat every day the words of the virtuous Palatine: *Malo periculosam libertatem quam quietum servitium* in their civic lives daily.
The Palatine of Poznań was the father of the king of Poland and Duke of Lorraine.
If a nation of gods existed, its government would surely be democratic. But this form is too perfect for human beings.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. V. Of an Aristocracy.
paragraphs: Under this form two moral persons are plainly distinguishable, the administration and the sovereign, and so there are two general wills: one that concerns all the citizens, and one that concerns only the members of the administration. Thus, although the government may order the internal policing of the state as it likes, it can speak to the people only in the sovereign's name, that is, in the name of the people themselves, a fact that must never be forgotten. The earliest human societies were governed by aristocracy. Heads of families discussed public matters among themselves, and the young readily deferred to the authority of experience. This is the origin of the names Priests, Fathers, Senate, and the like. The savages of North America are still governed in this way today, and very well governed they are.

As inequality created by social institutions began to outweigh natural differences, wealth and power took precedence over age, and aristocracy became elective. Eventually power passed along with property from father to son, making entire families patrician and turning government into an inheritance; boys of twenty became senators.
Among the ancients, the word “optimates” plainly meant not the best people but the most powerful.

Aristocracy, then, comes in three kinds: natural, by election, and by inheritance. The natural kind fits only the most primitive societies; the hereditary kind is the poorest of all governments. Election gives the best, and that is the one properly called aristocracy.

Besides the advantage of distinguishing those kinds, this form has the benefit of choosing who will govern. In a popular government every citizen is born a magistrate; here their number is strictly limited, and they reach office only by election. Their honesty, abilities, experience, and other qualities that earn public respect provide an additional assurance that the people will be wisely governed.

It is vital for the law to set the rules for choosing magistrates. Leave the choice to the prince and hereditary aristocracy becomes unavoidable, as happened in Venice and Berne. The first republic has long since disappeared, while the second has survived through the Senate’s great prudence. But this is an exception as dangerous as it is honourable.

Public assemblies also have greater decorum under this system; state matters are discussed more regularly and business is carried out with greater order and speed. In foreign eyes, the state’s standing is better served by a select group of respected senators than by a disorderly or contemptible crowd.

In a word, the best and most natural arrangement would certainly be for a small group of wise, experienced people to direct the multitude—if only we could be certain that they would govern for the majority’s benefit, not their own. There is no point in multiplying sources of action unnecessarily or having twenty thousand people do what a hundred carefully chosen people could do much better.

The conditions needed for this form differ from those for democracy. The state should not be so small, nor its people so simple or virtuous, that carrying out the laws naturally matches the public will, as it can in a well-established democracy. Yet the state should not be so large that its governors, spread across the provinces, can make themselves independent of the sovereign in their separate regions.

Although aristocracy needs fewer virtues than popular government, it needs some qualities of its own: restraint among the rich and contentment among the poor. Exact equality of circumstances would be quite unsuitable here, and even Sparta did not have it.

If some inequality of wealth is fitting in this government, the reason is that public affairs should generally be entrusted to people who can give the work their time—not, as Aristotle claims, because the rich should always be preferred simply for being rich. On the contrary, the people should sometimes see an opposite choice, so they learn that more important reasons for preference exist than wealth alone as a ground for selecting officeholders.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. VI. On monarchy.
paragraphs: Up to now we have thought of the prince as a collective, moral person, created by the force of the laws and holding the executive power of the state. Our task now is to examine that power when it rests in a physical person, an actual human being, entitled to wield it in accordance with the laws. This person bears the title of monarch or king.

In other forms of administration, a collective body represents a single person. Here the reverse happens: one person represents a collective body. The moral unity called the prince is also a physical unity, in which all the abilities combined by law in the former are naturally joined in the latter.

The people’s will, the prince’s will, the state’s public force, and the government’s particular force all depend on one source of action. All the machine’s parts are controlled by the same hand and directed towards the same end; nothing moves against anything else to obstruct and cancel its work. No other kind of government, it seems, can produce so much action with so little effort. Archimedes, sitting comfortably on shore and moving a great ship across the ocean at will, calls to my mind a capable monarch in his cabinet, directing distant provinces by keeping everything in motion while appearing still himself. Yet although no other government is so active, none gives such control to the personal will of one individual. Everything may move towards one end, but that end is not the public’s happiness. The administration’s power therefore works without pause to the state’s harm.

Kings want absolute power, and are sometimes told that the best way to obtain it is to earn the people’s love. This is an excellent principle and true in some respects, but sadly the courts laugh at it. Power grounded in popular affection is undoubtedly the greatest kind, yet it is so uncertain and conditional that princes have never been content with it. Even the best kings want the option of doing wrong whenever they please without giving up their prerogatives. It is useless for an eloquent political writer to tell them that a strong people makes them strong, and that a flourishing, numerous, respected population is in their greatest interest. They know that is not so. Their immediate private interest is for the people to be so weak and miserable that they cannot resist the government. I admit that, if the people were held in complete submission, the prince would benefit from their wealth and strength, because their power would also make him respected by neighbouring states. But that interest is secondary, and the two conditions cannot both be secured. It is natural, then, for princes to prefer the principle that offers the most immediate benefit. Samuel made this point forcefully to the Hebrews, and Machiavelli demonstrated it. While seeming to instruct kings, he gave the people the sharpest lessons; his book *The Prince* is especially useful to republics.

We have already shown, from the general relations among things, that monarchy suits only large states, and a closer look will convince us of this still more. The more members a public administration has, the weaker becomes the relation between prince and subjects, and the nearer it comes to nothing, to that equality which prevails in a democracy. The relation grows as the government shrinks, and reaches its greatest when the administration is in a single man's hands. Then the distance between prince and people is too great, and the state lacks cohesion. To fill that gap, intermediate ranks are needed, and so we get the various orders of nobility. Nothing of this kind suits a small state, which is ruined by these separate ranks.
If governing a state is difficult under any form, it is especially difficult for one person alone. Everyone knows what happens when a king rules through substitutes in real life in daily practice.

There is another essential and unavoidable flaw that will always put monarchical government below republican government. In a republic, popular choice seldom puts anyone into high office except men of knowledge and ability, who perform their duties creditably. Those who rise to such posts in monarchies, by contrast, are usually petty schemers and small minds, whose small talents, the sort that win favour at court, bring them to eminence as soon as they reach it, and then reveal their unfitness. People make fewer mistakes in selecting officials than a prince does; a minister of true merit at a royal court is as unusual as an imbecile at the head of a republic. If a lucky accident ever puts at the head of a monarchy, already brought almost to ruin by its swarm of minor administrators, someone who was born to govern, the country is amazed at what he accomplishes, and his term marks a new period in its history.

For a monarchy to be governed well, its size must match the ruler’s abilities. Conquest is easier than government. With a sufficiently long lever, one finger could move the earth, but supporting it would take the shoulders of Hercules. Whenever a state deserves to be called great, its prince is almost always too small for it. Should the opposite occur, though it seldom does, and the state be too little for its master, it will still be badly ruled: the leader’s grand ideas make him forget the people’s interests, and he harms them by misusing his excessive abilities just as another ruler might harm them by lacking the abilities required. A kingdom would therefore have to contract and expand with each succession, according to the new prince’s capacity. A senate’s abilities are more fixed, so under a republic the state can be set within definite limits, larger or smaller, and government can remain equally good. The clearest disadvantage of one-person rule is its failure to provide a continuous succession, which in the other two forms preserves an unbroken connection within the state. When a king dies, another must take his place. If kings are elected, however, each election creates a turbulent and dangerous interval. Unless citizens possess an unselfishness and honesty incompatible with this kind of government, bribery and corruption will necessarily take hold. The person who buys the state will almost always sell it again, making the weak repay the money he extorted from the strong. Under this system everyone eventually becomes corrupt and available for purchase. Even the calm that people enjoy under kings is worse than the disorder of an interregnum.

To deal with these problems, crowns have become hereditary, with a line of succession meant to prevent disputes when a king dies. This trades the problem of elections for the problem of regencies, choosing apparent calm over wise administration. People prefer the risk of a throne occupied by children, monsters, or fools to any dispute about choosing a good king. They fail to see that almost every chance is against the state when it faces this choice.

Nearly everything conspires to keep someone raised from childhood to command others from learning reason and justice. Great effort, people say, goes into teaching young princes the art of ruling, yet they do not seem to learn much from their lessons. It would be better to teach them first how to obey. The greatest monarchs in history were not trained to rule. Those taught this supposed science best often know it least; obedience teaches it better than command. As the saying goes, the most useful and shortest way to judge what is good or bad is to consider what one would or would not want from another ruler.

This lack of continuity makes royal government inconsistent: one policy is followed, then another, depending on the character of the prince or of those who govern in his name. Its conduct changes as often as its aims. The state moves from one principle and plan to another. Other forms of government do not have this uncertainty, since the prince remains the same. In general, a court may have more cunning, but a senate has more genuine wisdom. Republics pursue their ends through more consistent means. Every change in a court’s ministry brings a change in the state, because nearly every minister and king makes a point of reversing the policies of his immediate predecessor. This same inconsistency also exposes a common trick of royal politicians: they compare civil government to the rule of a household and the prince to a father, an error I have already addressed; then they freely grant the reigning ruler every virtue he needs and simply assume he is what he ought to be. On that assumption monarchy clearly seems better than all other forms because it is unquestionably the strongest. To make it the best as well, all that is required is that the prince’s will agree with the general will of the people It also lets them treat the comparison as proof instead of examining the actual conditions of royal rule. If we grant the prince the qualities he ought to have, we have quietly replaced the real person with an ideal one. The argument then says nothing about the ordinary monarchs who hold power.

Yet if, as Plato holds, the king by nature is so rare a person, how seldom must nature and fortune come together to put him on the throne? And if a royal upbringing necessarily corrupts whoever receives it, what are we to expect from a succession of men brought up that way? It is therefore a deliberate mistake to confuse monarchy as such with the rule of a good king. To see what this kind of government is in itself, we have to look at it under weak or wicked princes, for such they are when they come to the throne, or such the throne makes them. A few writers have seen these difficulties yet appear untroubled by them. Their cure, they say, is submission without a murmur: God sends bad rulers in his anger, and we should endure them as heaven's punishment. Such talk is no doubt edifying, but I think it belongs better in a pulpit than in a book on politics. What should we say of a physician who promised miracles and whose entire art consisted in urging his patients to be patient and resigned? When we live under a bad government we plainly have to put up with it; what we need to learn is how to obtain a good one.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. VII. Of mixed Governments.
paragraphs: Strictly speaking, no government is truly simple. Even a sole ruler needs subordinate magistrates, and even a popular government needs a leader. Executive power is therefore always arranged in levels, from the larger number down to the smaller, though sometimes the larger group depends on the smaller and sometimes the reverse is true.

The levels are sometimes equal, either because their constituent parts depend on one another, as in England, or because each part’s authority is independent, though incomplete, as in Poland. The latter is a poor form of government, since its parts are not united and the state lacks a proper connection between them.
Politicians argue at length over whether simple or mixed government is better. I would give the same answer I already gave to the related question about forms of government in general.

Simple government is best in itself, if for no other reason than that it is simple. But when executive power is not sufficiently subordinate to the legislature—when the gap between prince and sovereign is greater than the gap between people and prince—the defect must be corrected by dividing the government. Each part can then retain its authority over subjects, while their division makes them less able collectively to resist the sovereign.

The same problem can also be addressed by establishing several subordinate magistrates. They maintain a balance between the two powers and protect each one’s proper authority. In this case the government is not truly mixed; it is simply moderated.

The same methods can correct the opposite problem, when government is too weak, by creating suitable bodies that gather its force together. All democracies use this approach. In one case the administration is divided to make it weaker; in the other it is concentrated to strengthen it. Simple governments can reach either extreme of strength or weakness, while mixed forms place them at an intermediate balance.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. VIII. That every form of government is not equally proper for every country.
paragraphs: Liberty is not produced by every climate, and every people cannot achieve it to the same degree. The more we reflect on this principle, which Montesquieu established, the more convincing it becomes. The more people dispute it, the more new evidence confirms it.

Under any government, the political body—the public—consumes but produces nothing. Where, then, does it get what it uses? From the work of its members. Public needs are supplied by what individuals produce beyond their own needs. A society can therefore last only as long as its members’ work produces such a surplus.

The size of that surplus varies between countries. It is very large in some, modest in others, nonexistent in some, and even less than nothing in a few. The balance depends on soil and climate, the work needed to cultivate the land, what it produces, the strength of its people, what they need to live, and many similar factors.

Governments also differ in kind: some consume far more than others. Their difference comes from this principle: the farther public contributions must travel from the source that paid them, the more burdensome they become. We should judge a tax not by its amount but by how long it takes, and how difficult it is, for the money to return to the hands from which it was collected. When this return is quick and easy, the tax may be large or small without much consequence: the people remain prosperous and public finances healthy. But even a low tax will soon exhaust a population if its money never comes back to them. Such a state cannot become wealthy, and its people will remain poor.

The farther the people live from the seat of government, the heavier their taxes become. They weigh least in a democracy, more in an aristocracy, and most in a monarchy. Monarchy is therefore suited only to wealthy nations, aristocracy to those of moderate means, and democracy to poorer countries relative to other nations at the source.

The more we consider this point, the clearer the difference between a monarchy and a free state becomes. In the latter, all its strength serves the public good. In the former, the state’s public interest and the prince’s private interest oppose one another: one grows as the other shrinks. Rather than governing subjects so they can be happy, despotism makes them miserable to keep them governable as an institution for the public.

In every climate, then, we can trace natural causes that indicate which form of government suits it best and even what kind of people should live there. Barren, unproductive land, where crops cannot repay the labour of farming, would remain empty and uncultivated—or at best would be inhabited only by people living without settled society. Countries that provide only enough for basic survival would be home to uncivilized peoples, among whom civil government could not be established. Places offering a moderate surplus would suit a free people best. Fertile plains and rich valleys, where farmers receive a generous return, would suit monarchy, so that the prince’s luxury could consume the subjects’ surplus; it is better for government to spend that surplus than for individuals to waste it. I know that exceptions to this view can be raised, but they confirm the general rule: sooner or later, they lead to upheavals that restore things to their natural order in the same country in time.

We should always separate general rules from the particular causes that can change their effects. Even if the southern countries were all republics and the northern ones despotic monarchies, the theory would still hold that, considering climate alone, despotism best suits hot regions, a simple uncultivated life cold ones, and good political order temperate ones. The application can still be disputed even if we accept the principle. Someone may point out that some cold countries are fertile, while some warmer southern lands are barren. That objection matters only if we fail to examine the whole question. As I said earlier, we must take account of people’s labour, their strength, their needs, and every other relevant condition.

Suppose two countries have the same area and produce in the ratio of five to ten. If the people in the first consume four parts and those in the second consume nine, each has a surplus of one. Since their surplus is also inversely proportional to their production, the country yielding only five will have nearly twice the excess of the one yielding ten overall, in this example.

The argument does not depend on one country producing twice as much as another. In fact, I doubt that cold countries generally match the fertility of warmer ones. Still, suppose their yields are equal: compare England with Sicily, or Poland with Egypt. Farther south lie Africa and India; to the north there is hardly anything. Yet producing this equal yield requires very different labour! In Sicily, people need only turn the soil, while farming in England is extremely demanding. When more workers are needed to produce the same yield, the surplus must be smaller because cultivation takes more work even when the work is difficult.

Add that equal populations eat much less in a hot climate than in a cold one. People must eat moderately in the heat if they want to stay healthy. Europeans see the effects when those who keep their usual diet in hot countries die every day from dysentery and indigestion. Chardin describes Europeans as predators, almost wolves beside the people of Asia. He thinks writers are wrong to explain Persian moderation by saying their country is uncultivated. Instead, he says it is poorly cultivated because the people need little to live on. If they ate little only because their land was barren, then only the poor would eat little. But restraint is common to all Persians. Nor would it be equally widespread across provinces with different levels of infertility, yet their frugality is found throughout the kingdom. Chardin also says Persians praise their way of life, claiming their complexions alone show it is better than the Christian way. He agrees that their skin is smooth, soft, and polished, while Armenians under Persian rule, who follow European habits, have rough, spotty complexions and heavier, less agile bodies He supports this by comparing customs and bodies across communities. He notes the pattern is widespread.

The closer people live to the equator, the more moderate their diet tends to be. They scarcely eat meat; rice and corn are their usual foods. Millions in India live on food worth less than a penny a day. Even in Europe we see a clear difference between north and south: a Spaniard can live for a week on what a German eats at one meal. Where people eat a great deal, luxury also consumes more. In England it appears as many courses and large portions of meat; in Italy, a meal is dressed up with sweets and flowers These examples are used to support his broader claim about consumption and climate.

Clothing shows similar differences. Where the weather changes suddenly and severely, people wear better but plainer clothes. Where they dress mainly for display, brilliance matters more than usefulness and clothing itself becomes a luxury. In Naples one sees gentlemen walking about each day in embroidered clothes and no stockings. Buildings follow the same pattern: people care chiefly about grandeur where the weather poses little threat. In Paris and London they want warm, comfortable rooms. Madrid has magnificent halls but no window frames or panes, and the beds are exposed to rats living in the roof across the seasons.

Food in hot countries is also more substantial and nourishing than in cold ones; this is a third difference that affects the previous one. Why do Italians eat so many vegetables? Because their vegetables are tasty and good. In France, where people themselves are nourished mainly by water, vegetables are less nutritious and considered unimportant, though they take up just as much land and work to grow. It has been shown by experiment that grain from Barbary, though otherwise inferior to French grain, yields more flour, and French grain yields more than grain from northern regions. We can infer that the same downward progression continues from equator to pole. Is it not an obvious disadvantage to get less food from the same harvest?

To these points I can add another that follows from them and confirms the argument: hot countries need fewer inhabitants than cold ones but can feed more, creating a double surplus that always favours despotism. When the same number of people are spread over a large area, rebellion is harder. They cannot assemble easily or in secret, and the government can readily break up their associations and ruin their plans. But the more densely a large population gathers, the less power government can claim over the sovereign. Faction leaders can meet as safely as the prince’s council, and a crowd can gather in public squares as easily as troops in their barracks. A tyrannical government therefore benefits from acting at a distance. Like a lever, its strength grows with distance when it has a suitable pivot. The people, by contrast, act only when brought together; spread out, their force dissipates like gunpowder scattered over the ground, which burns one grain at a time without producing an effect. Tyrants flourish most in thinly populated countries; only wilderness belongs to wild beasts.

This does not contradict what I argued in Book II, Chapter IX, about the disadvantages of large states. There I discussed government’s authority over its members; here the subject is its influence over its subjects. Officials scattered across different places give government points from which it can act at a distance on the people, but they provide no such supports for controlling the officials themselves. In the first case the long lever gives strength; in the second it creates weakness.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. IX. Of the marks of a good Government.
paragraphs: Asked in general terms which form of government is best, the question is impossible to answer because it is so vague. It may have as many reasonable answers as there are combinations of the fixed and changing circumstances of a people.
But asking what signs show whether a particular people are governed well or badly is a different matter. That is a definite question of fact, and it can be settled.

In practice, though, people never settle it, because each answers in his own way. A subject praises public order; a citizen, individual liberty. One values the safety of property, another personal security. One calls the strictest government best; another prefers the most agreeable. One wants crimes punished, another prevented. One thinks it glorious to frighten neighbouring states; another would rather those states did not know he existed. One is content if money circulates, another insists that the people have bread. Even agreement on these points and others like them would not bring us much closer to settling the argument. Moral matters cannot be measured with precision. People may agree about which sign to use and still disagree about how to interpret it.

I am surprised that so plain a sign could be misunderstood, or that anyone could be dishonest enough not to admit it. What is the purpose of political society? Surely to protect its members and help them prosper. What most reliably proves that this is happening? The number of people and the growth of the population. We need look no further for the disputed test. If all else is equal, and the increase does not come from immigrants becoming citizens or new colonies being founded, the best government must be the one under which the people grow and multiply most. Conversely, all else being equal, the worst is the one under which their number declines. Once we accept this, answering the question is a matter of calculation, which I will leave to the mathematicians.

We should apply the same principle when judging which periods deserve to be called most prosperous for humanity. We have generally praised times when literature and the fine arts flourished without uncovering the hidden causes of that growth or weighing its deadly consequences: *idque apud imperitos humanitas vocabatur, cum pars servitutis esset*. Can we never see through the maxims in books to the interests of the people who wrote them? Whatever authors may claim, if a country’s population is falling, things are not going well, regardless of its wealth and outward splendour. A poet earning a hundred thousand livres a year does not thereby make his age the best of all ages. We should care less about the world’s apparent calm and the quiet of its rulers than about the well-being of whole nations, especially the most populous ones. A hailstorm may ruin a few provinces without usually causing famine. Temporary riots and civil wars may greatly trouble rulers without being the true miseries of a people; people may even get a respite while they argue over who will tyrannize them. Real prosperity or misery lies in their lasting condition. When everyone meekly accepts the yoke, that is when everyone is dying; then the rulers destroy them at their leisure, and *ubi solitudinem faciunt pacem appellant*. During the turmoil of the noble factions in France, when the coadjutor of Paris went into parliament with a dagger in his pocket, the French people as a whole continued to multiply and to live in contentment and comfort. Ancient Greece flourished during the cruellest wars: rivers of blood were spilled, yet the land was full of people. Machiavelli says that despite murders, executions, and civil wars, the Roman republic only grew stronger: citizens’ courage, customs, and independence did more to strengthen it than its conflicts did to weaken it. A little unrest gives the mind energy. Liberty, not peace, is the true source of human prosperity.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. X. Of the abuse of government, and its tendency to degenerate.
paragraphs: The prince's own will continually opposes the general will of the people, and so the government is always striving against the sovereign. The harder it strives, the more the constitution is altered. Since in this situation no other corporate will exists to balance the prince's will, sooner or later the prince is bound to overpower the sovereign and shatter the social treaty. This is the flaw built into the political body, one that from its birth drives it constantly toward its end, just as old age and death drive the human body toward its own.

A government can degrade in two main ways: by contracting, or by the dissolution of the state. Contraction means a shift from a large number of rulers to a small one: democracy gives way to aristocracy, and aristocracy to the rule of a single king. That is the course it naturally follows. If it moved the other way and its membership grew, one could say it was loosening or expanding, but such a reverse movement cannot happen.

The gradual rise and development of Venice’s republic gives a notable example of this sequence. It is astonishing that in 1,200 years the Venetians advanced no further than its second stage, which began in 1198. As for the early doges, often criticized as part of its constitution, they were certainly not sovereigns, whatever some writers may claim.
The Roman republic may seem to contradict my argument, since it appears to have moved from monarchy to aristocracy and then from aristocracy to democracy. I do not think that is what truly happened.

The first constitution of Romulus was a mixed one, and it quickly degenerated into despotism. For unusual reasons the state died before its time, like an infant who dies before reaching adulthood. The expulsion of the Tarquins truly marks the republic’s beginning, though it did not immediately take a settled form, because the change was only half complete: the patrician order remained. An inherited aristocracy—the worst form of government—therefore opposed democracy, and the constitution stayed unsettled. As Machiavelli observes, it was not fixed until the tribunes were established. Only then did the state have a genuine government in the form of a true democracy. At that point the people were not only sovereign but also magistrates and judges. The Senate was a lower court, intended to moderate and organize government. Even the consuls, though patricians and chief magistrates who held absolute command as generals in the field, were in Rome merely presidents of the people’s assemblies.

From then on, the government plainly followed its natural course and moved strongly toward aristocracy. As the patrician order died out, aristocracy no longer rested in that group, as it had in Venice and Genoa; it took shape in the Senate, whose members included patricians and common people, and even among the tribunes once they began to seize active power. A change of words does not change the facts: whenever people have leaders who govern in their place, whatever those leaders are called, the government is aristocratic. Abuse of this form produced civil wars and the triumvirate. Sylla, Julius Caesar, and Augustus did become true monarchs, and under Tiberius’s despotism the state was finally dissolved. Roman history therefore confirms my principle instead of disproving it.

Government never changes its form unless its driving force has become too worn to sustain it. If that force weakens further because it is spread too widely, it becomes powerless and even less able to support itself. It must therefore be tightened and renewed as it slackens; otherwise the state that depends on it must fall.

The state can be dissolved in two ways. First, the prince may stop governing under the law and claim sovereign power for himself. This radically changes the state: what contracts is not merely the government but the state itself. The great state then dissolves, and another forms within it, made up only of government members, who become masters and tyrants over everyone else. The instant government usurps sovereignty, the social compact is broken. People who were citizens regain their natural liberty and obey from force, not from any legal obligation by its officials there.

The same thing happens when individual government members seize separately a power they may exercise only together. This violates the law just as much and produces even worse results. There are then as many princes as magistrates, and the state, divided no less than the government, is wholly dissolved or takes on a new form.

When the state breaks up, the abuse of government of whatever sort goes by the general name of anarchy. To be more exact, democracy is said to decay into ochlocracy, and aristocracy into oligarchy; To these I might add tyranny as the decay of monarchy, though that word is ambiguous and calls for an explanation. Commonly, a tyrant means a king who governs by force and pays no attention to justice or law. In the stricter sense, it is any person who takes royal power without having a right to it. That is how the Greeks understood the word, and they applied it without distinction to good and bad princes whose authority was not lawful. Tyrant and usurper are therefore perfectly equivalent terms.

*Omnes enim et habentur et dicuntur tyranni qui potestate utuntur perpetuâ, in eâ civitate quae libertate usa est. CORN. NEPOS. IN MILTIADE.* Aristotle does distinguish king from tyrant by saying that one governs for his own benefit and the other for the benefit of his subjects. But Greek writers generally use “tyrant” differently, as is clear in Xenophon’s *Hieron*. Following Aristotle’s distinction would imply that no king has ever existed anywhere in the world.

To give different names to different things, I call the unlawful seizure of royal authority tyranny, and the unlawful seizure of sovereign power despotism. A tyrant unlawfully takes the job of governing under the laws; a despot places himself above the laws themselves. A tyrant need not be a despot, but every despotic ruler is necessarily a tyrant.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. XI. Of the dissolution of the body politic.
paragraphs: Even the best-designed governments naturally and inevitably tend to decline. If Rome and Sparta fell, what state can expect to live forever? When we try to create durable institutions, we should not imagine that we can make them eternal. To have any hope of success, we must avoid trying to do the impossible or pretend that human institutions can last in a way their nature does not allow.

The political body, like the human body, begins dying at the moment it is born and carries the causes of its destruction within it. Each may nevertheless have a stronger or weaker constitution suited to a longer or shorter life. Nature makes the human constitution; the state’s constitution is made by art. People cannot lengthen their own lives, but they can extend the life of a state as far as possible by giving it a constitution best suited to endure. Even the most perfect constitution will eventually end, but much later than others unless some unforeseen event brings it to a premature close.

The source of political life is sovereign authority. Legislative power is the state’s heart; executive power is its brain, setting every part in motion. A stroke can disable the brain while the person remains alive. Someone may become helpless and unaware and still go on living. But when the heart stops beating, the animal is dead.

The state survives through legislative power, not simply through the existence of laws. Yesterday’s statutes do not necessarily bind today by themselves; their continued force is presumed from the legislature’s silence, as if the sovereign kept confirming every law it had not actually repealed. Whatever the sovereign once declared to be its will remains so unless that will is withdrawn.

Why, then, do people show such respect for old laws? For this reason: it is reasonable to assume that their lasting presence can only be explained by their excellence. If the sovereign had not continually found them helpful and sound, it would have repealed them.

We can therefore see that in a well-formed state, laws gain authority over time instead of losing their force. Their age makes people more respectful of them every day. In a country where laws instead grow old, fall out of use, and lose their power, that is itself proof that the legislative authority has declined and the state is already dead.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. XII. By what means the sovereign authority is maintained.
paragraphs: The sovereign has no force except the legislative power, so it acts only through laws; and since laws are nothing but authentic acts of the general will, the sovereign can act only when the people are assembled. The people assembled! you will exclaim. What a wild notion that is. It is a wild notion today, but it was not thought one two thousand years ago. Has human nature changed since then?

The possible in moral and political matters reaches farther than we tend to think. Our weaknesses, vices, and prejudices are what restrict it. Small-minded people distrust the feelings of heroic minds, while slaves mock the very idea of liberty.

We can judge what may be done again by what has already been done. I will not discuss the small republics of ancient Greece. Rome was certainly a great state, and Rome itself a great city. In the last census of Roman citizens, 400,000 men were counted as fit to bear arms. The final census of the empire counted more than four million citizens, not including subjects, women, children, or slaves.

You may ask how difficult it must have been to assemble the people of that capital and the surrounding area so often. Yet hardly a week went by without a meeting of the Roman people, and sometimes they met several times in a week. This vast assembly exercised sovereign functions and sometimes governed as well. At some meetings it debated state affairs; at others it decided legal cases. The entire people gathered in public almost as often to act as magistrates as to act as citizens.

If we look back to the earliest nations, we find that most ancient governments, including monarchies such as Macedon, had similar popular assemblies. In any case, once the fact is proved beyond dispute, it removes the difficulty: no one can object to showing that something is possible by proving that it has actually happened.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. XIII. The subject continued.
paragraphs: It is not enough for the people to assemble once, establish the state’s constitution, and approve a code of laws. It is not enough to set up a permanent government or make a single choice of magistrates for all time. Alongside extraordinary meetings required by unforeseen events, the people need regular, scheduled assemblies that no one can cancel or postpone. On a certain day, the law itself must summon them, with no special statute needed to call the meeting formally.

Outside these regular assemblies, whose date makes them lawful, every other meeting should be considered illegal unless the proper magistrate, already appointed for this purpose, calls it using the prescribed process. All decisions from an unauthorized meeting must be treated as void, because the law itself must define how the people are to assemble.

How often lawful assemblies should be held depends on so many circumstances that no exact rule can be laid down. All one can say in general is that the stronger a government is, the more often the sovereign ought to show itself.

Someone may say that this works well enough for one town or city, but ask what should happen in a state made up of several cities. Should sovereign power be divided among them, or should it be placed in one city, with all the others wholly subject to it?

I answer: neither. First, sovereign authority is single and uniform; dividing it would destroy it. Second, one city cannot lawfully be subject to another, any more than one nation can be subject to another. The political body exists through the union of obedience and liberty. “Subject” and “sovereign” are complementary terms that come together in the single idea of a citizen as citizens.

I would add that joining several towns to make one city is fundamentally wrong, and once such a union exists its natural disadvantages must follow. We should not use the special problems of large states to attack the position of someone who insists on the unique benefits of small ones. But how, someone may ask, can small states become strong enough to resist great powers? In the way the ancient Greek cities resisted a mighty king, and in more recent times Switzerland and Holland resisted the power of the House of Austria.

If a state cannot be kept within suitable boundaries, there is one option: do not allow a permanent capital. Move the seat of government from city to city, and convene the country’s assemblies in each place in turn.

People the country evenly from one end to the other; spread the same rights and advantages throughout it. The state will then become both strongest and best governed. Remember that city walls rest on the ruins of villages, and that magnificent town palaces are built at the expense of miserable country cottages.

chapters.title: Book III. CHAP. XIV. Subject continued.
paragraphs: As soon as the people lawfully assemble as a sovereign body, government’s authority stops and the state’s executive power is suspended. The least important citizen’s person becomes as sacred and untouchable as the highest magistrate’s, because when those being represented are present, their representatives are no longer needed. Most of the disturbances at Rome’s comitia came from people generally misunderstanding or ignoring this rule. At those meetings the consuls merely chaired the people’s assembly, the tribunes only spoke for it, and the Senate had no role at all.

This means almost the same as those who speak on a matter in the British Parliament. The similarity between their roles set consuls and tribunes against one another, even while their authority was suspended.

These moments when power is suspended—when the prince recognizes, or should recognize, an actual superior—have always frightened rulers.
